It held the BCO uses 'minister' synonymously with pastor and teaching elder, but is silent on general use for non-ordained staff; a lower court may exercise discretion subject to BCO 40-2(3)'s WESP review. The decision addressed only the constitutional issue, not the title's wisdom or propriety; four commissioners dissented.
2007-13.disposition_detail: Complaint denied; BCO meaning and generic use of title distinguished; dissent recorded
2007-13.standard_of_review_detail: The SJC interpreted BCO terminology and reserved generic-title propriety to lower-court judgment under BCO 40-2(3).

2008-16.summary: Ministers challenged Presbytery’s handling of RE Payne’s confession as a BCO 38-1 case without process, asking the SJC to declare it incomplete and require prosecution of additional alleged sins. The SJC did not sustain the complaint. It held that a complaint cannot bypass the BCO 33-1 and 34-1 procedures by seeking relief akin to original jurisdiction. Further allegations could be filed as formal charges with Payne’s Session, which could investigate, prosecute, or reference the matter to a higher court.
2008-16.disposition_detail: Complaint denied; presbytery's handling of confession and indefinite suspension affirmed
2008-16.standard_of_review_detail: The SJC treated the presbytery's disciplinary judgment as discretionary and did not find clear error.

2009-05.summary: Four complainants challenged Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its finding of no strong presumption of guilt, citing delayed action and failure to interview accusers. The SJC denied the complaints: BCO 31-2 requires due diligence but grants great discretion and prescribes neither interviews nor a timetable, and the record showed no clear constitutional error overcoming deference to Presbytery. Lyons and Woodward also lacked standing because they were not under Presbytery’s jurisdiction. No renewed investigation or process was ordered.
2009-05.disposition_detail: Specifications not sustained; BCO 31-2 investigation and no-strong-presumption finding affirmed
2009-05.standard_of_review_detail: The SJC expressly applied great deference to the lower court's investigative discretion under BCO 39-3(3).

2009-06.summary: Pacific Northwest Presbytery adopted a report finding TE Peter Leithart's views not out of accord with the fundamentals of the system of doctrine. The SJC sustained a complaint, holding PNW erred because, without formal judicial process, it lacked authority to declare either that the views were out of accord or that they were not. The record still suggested a strong presumption of guilt. The SJC refused complainants' affirmative declaration and remanded with directions for pastoral counsel under BCO 31-7 and possible BCO 31-2 compliance.
2009-06.disposition_detail: Complaint sustained; presbytery's declaration reversed and matter remanded for counsel or BCO 31-2 action
2009-06.standard_of_review_detail: The case combined constitutional interpretation of doctrinal conformity with deferential review of investigative procedure.

2010-14.title: Michael A. McNeil v. Chesapeake Presbytery
2010-14.summary: The SJC reported McNeil’s complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery as judicially out of order. The published status notice supplies no explanation for that ruling or substantive account of the dispute.
2010-14.disposition_detail: Complaint found judicially out of order; no reason or merits decision published
2010-14.standard_of_review_detail: The published status notice records a judicially out-of-order ruling without reaching the merits.

2006-04.summary: The Assembly record reports that complaint 2006-04 against Heritage Presbytery was found out of order. The published stub does not identify the challenged presbytery action, classify the ruling as administrative or judicial, state a reason, or provide a merits determination or relief. The case therefore supports only that procedural disposition, not a substantive rule.
2006-04.disposition_detail: Out of order; matter not heard on the merits
2006-04.standard_of_review_detail: The matter ended procedurally before a merits standard of review was required.

2010-02.summary: The 38th General Assembly recorded Cutler v. Platte Valley as administratively out of order. The published stub identifies neither the challenged action nor the circumstances supporting that ruling and contains no separate merits opinion. It therefore supports only the administrative disposition, not a merits determination or case-specific rule.
2010-02.disposition_detail: Administratively out of order; no merits decision
2010-02.standard_of_review_detail: The matter ended procedurally before a merits standard of review was required.

2010-25.summary: The published record identifies Mr. Peter Yuan’s matter against South Coast Presbytery only as administratively out of order. It does not identify the challenged action, procedural vehicle, administrative defect, merits determination, relief, or further proceedings. Accordingly, the case supports only this procedural disposition, not any substantive rule or outcome.
2010-25.disposition_detail: Administratively out of order; no merits decision
2010-25.standard_of_review_detail: The matter ended procedurally before a merits standard of review was required.

2017-13.summary: A complaint by RE Michael Tripp against Ohio Valley Presbytery ended when the SJC noted it was withdrawn. No separate merits opinion was published, and the adopted note supplies no reasons or ruling on the presbytery action. The only stated result is withdrawal; no relief was granted or denied on the merits. Because the stub does not describe the challenged conduct, the case is useful only as a short-record withdrawal status.
2017-13.disposition_detail: Withdrawn before decision; no merits disposition
2017-13.standard_of_review_detail: The matter ended before the SJC reached the merits.

2022-14.summary: The SJC dismissed Oh’s complaint against Korean Southeast Presbytery following his withdrawal of it. The brief decision does not identify the challenged presbytery action, address the merits, or grant substantive relief.
2022-14.disposition_detail: Complaint withdrawn; dismissed without merits decision
2022-14.standard_of_review_detail: The complaint ended by withdrawal before merits review was required.

1981-02.summary: A ruling elder complained that the Presbytery of Texas, handling a complaint against a session, appointed a committee rather than the requested commission and had that committee meet with the pastor, session members, and congregants before meeting the complainants. The Assembly adopted the Judicial Commission's report and unanimously confirmed the lower court's judgment (10-0). No adopted reasons or issue-level merits appear, so the case's value is a sparse example of a confirmed judgment without explanation.

1992-09a.disposition_detail: Licensure challenge not sustained; complaint sustained as to the unlicensed stated-supply service
1992-09a.summary: Antioch Session challenged Peterson’s licensure based on his prior divorce, creation and local-flood views, reversal of a committee recommendation, and close vote; it also challenged his regular preaching before licensure. The SJC rejected the licensure specifications because Presbytery had thoroughly examined repentance and doctrinal adherence, and no definitive PCA standard required exclusion on these facts. It sustained the pre-licensure supply issue under BCO 19-1, 22-5, and 22-6 and enjoined greater future circumspection. The licensure remained undisturbed; the ruling was expressly case-specific.

2000-08.disposition_detail: Complaint prematurely filed before Presbytery completed its action
2000-08.summary: The SJC found the Session’s complaint prematurely filed because Korean Capital Presbytery had not completed its action on it. The sparse ruling gives no merits determination or further relief.

2017-10.disposition_detail: Citation response accepted and materials referred to the Review of Presbytery Records Committee
2017-10.summary: The SJC found that Korean Eastern Presbytery complied with its citation by providing the materials required under BCO 40-1, then referred those materials to the Committee for Review of Presbytery Records. Compliance with the production requirement did not itself constitute substantive approval of the submitted records.

2017-11.disposition_detail: Citation responses accepted and forwarded to the Review of Presbytery Records Committee
2017-11.summary: The SJC accepted Korean Southwest Presbytery's responses, approved by the Presbytery, as complying with its citation. It forwarded them to the Review of Presbytery Records Committee. The sparse record identifies no underlying citation grounds, merits analysis, or separate opinion; the practical result was a finding of citation compliance and continued records review.

2017-12.disposition_detail: Citation responses accepted and forwarded to the Review of Presbytery Records Committee
2017-12.summary: The SJC unanimously accepted Platte Valley Presbytery's responses, which the Presbytery had approved, as complying with the SJC's citation. It noted that those responses and the requested minutes were forwarded to the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records. The entry does not disclose the underlying citation grounds or evaluate the presbytery's records on the merits; it confirms citation compliance and sends the materials on for ordinary records review.

2020-02.disposition_detail: BCO 34-1 requests answered by reference to Cases 2020-12 and 2020-05
2020-02.summary: The SJC answered three presbyteries' BCO 34-1 requests concerning Missouri Presbytery by reference to two Speck complaint decisions. One had upheld Missouri's decision not to indict on four allegations; the other had partly sustained a procedural and supervisory complaint and ordered a focused new hearing. The brief ruling gave no separate judgment or reasoning on the original-jurisdiction requests and did not transfer them to another court.

2020-04.disposition_detail: Complaint returned to Central Indiana Presbytery with instructions to reinvestigate under BCO 31-2
2020-04.summary: Marusich challenged Presbytery’s receipt of a commission’s finding that accusations against a teaching elder did not establish a strong presumption of guilt, and the commission’s failure to provide minutes or a full report. Without answering either issue or identifying an error, the SJC remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation, a narrative of the evidence, and a recommendation for Presbytery’s consideration under regular orders. The decision expressly establishes no general rule for BCO 31-2 investigations.

2022-11.disposition_detail: BCO 34-1 petitions answered and decided by reference to the final decision in Case 2022-10
2022-11.summary: The SJC had postponed BCO 34-1 petitions concerning Central Indiana Presbytery until the Herron trial concluded. After acquitting Herron on all charges and restoring him to good standing, the SJC answered and decided the petitions by reference to that final trial decision. The petitions were thus resolved through incorporation of the trial result, not transferred to another court; the trial itself arose from a distinct BCO 41 reference.

2022-12.disposition_detail: BCO 34-1 petitions dismissed for lack of jurisdiction after the minister and congregation left the PCA
2022-12.summary: The SJC dismissed two BCO 34-1 overtures asking the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction over alleged doctrinal errors by TE Greg Johnson. After Memorial Presbyterian Church withdrew from the PCA and Missouri Presbytery removed Johnson's name from its rolls under BCO 38-3a, the SJC held it lacked authority to assume original jurisdiction because the PCA no longer had jurisdiction over him. The dismissal did not resolve the doctrinal allegations; one commissioner dissented.

1975-01.summary: Ministers complained that Pacific Presbytery conducted nonroutine business without the constitutionally required quorum of three teaching and three ruling elders. The Assembly agreed that the August 4, 1975 actions were irregular, but dismissed the complaint because Presbytery later met with a quorum and ratified those actions. The dismissal therefore reflected correction of the defect, not approval of proceeding without a quorum.

1978-02.title: Luther L. Allin Jr. et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
1978-02.summary: Session members challenged Presbytery’s order to hold a congregational meeting on officer rotation and its handling of the complaint hearing. The Judicial Commission held that ten days ran from the notice’s postmark and that Bristow and Pastor Vitullo could not participate as members of the reviewing court. It nevertheless upheld Presbytery’s authority to require the meeting: a sufficient petition left the Session no option to refuse, while the congregation retained authority to decide rotation. The complaint was sustained in part and remanded for a properly noticed hearing.

1982-01.summary: A Session challenged Gulf Coast Presbytery’s refusal to sustain Raymond Bradford Fell’s ordination examination, contending that his theonomic view was improperly treated as disqualifying and that prejudicial materials affected the process. The General Assembly sustained specifications 1, 2, and 5, but not 3 and 4. It ordered re-examination after direct guidance on specific biblical and confessional deficiencies, while expressly refusing to dictate the result. It also urged that no view of the judicial law’s present application should itself define orthodoxy or heresy.

1982-03.summary: Teaching elders challenged Central Georgia Presbytery’s refusal to sustain a complaint against Liberty Presbyterian Church’s Session for closing a disciplinary matter before taking judicial action. The General Assembly sustained the complaint, adopting findings that counseling, Session discussion, and instruction on discipline were underway before the Session closed the matter and refused to reopen it. It requested Presbytery to assist the Session with appropriate corrections or further action and said both courts should heed confessional teaching on marriage and repentance. The complainants’ requested affirmations were not expressly ordered.

1982-06.summary: The Session challenged Presbytery’s refusal to receive complaints and associated voting, executive-session, elder-emeritus, interpretive, and disciplinary actions. The General Assembly sustained items 1, 2, and 5, but not 3, 4, and 6. Receiving a complaint under BCO 43-1 was not subject to a vote; when heard, complainants and respondents could not participate. Executive session was permissible, an elder emeritus retained full privileges, and item 6 was improper in this court. No reason was given for item 5. Presbytery was instructed to receive and hear the complaints properly.

1984-05.summary: Complaint challenged Ascension Presbytery's March 10, 1984 refusal to obey the Eleventh General Assembly's directive to correct constitutional defects in Kurt Lutjens's ordination trial, and its purported BCO 41 reference of the matter to the Twelfth General Assembly for retrial. The CJB sustained specifications of continued non-compliance and constitutional violation and adopted recommendations for remedial action. The complaint's asserted distinction—that BCO 41 cannot return a prior General Assembly decision for retrial—marks the case's practical limit.

1986-01.summary: Ministers challenged Calvary Presbytery's approval of William Hyer's examination and reception despite his belief that noncanonical, nonbinding revelation could continue. The Assembly sustained the complaint because PCA standards foreclose continuing revelation beyond illumination and providence. It annulled only the examination portion concerning revelation, suspending his reception, and instructed Presbytery to counsel and re-examine him, then report to the next Assembly. The majority deemed the record sufficient despite a dissent emphasizing Hyer's affirmation of Scripture's finality and the absence of an examination transcript.

1986-03.summary: A ruling elder challenged Palmetto Presbytery’s publication, as an appendix to meeting minutes, of a letter never discussed at that meeting, and its handling of his complaint. The Judicial Commission sustained specifications 1 and 3: Presbytery had not clearly declared the publication erroneous, and it risked harming Covenant’s Session. Specifications 2 and 4 failed because Presbytery timely referred the complaint, though its record was inaccurate, and acted in good faith. Despite Presbytery’s later deletion of the letter, the Commission remanded for a new hearing on specifications 1 and 3.

1986-05.summary: Five appellants challenged censures imposed after a Presbytery commission treated a Session's request for assistance as authority to initiate judicial process. The Assembly sustained all six specifications, holding that the commission lacked authority to proceed before charges were approved and that original jurisdiction remained with the Session. It reversed the censures, ordered their public removal, and remanded for the Session to address any properly specified charges. The ruling expressly did not determine the appellants' guilt or innocence.

1986-06.summary: Presbytery’s response claiming that Lutjens had changed his sacramental views was challenged as factually false and as a retroactive rewriting of minutes Presbytery had previously refused to interpret. All five specifications were sustained, including illegitimate interpretation of BCO 58-4. Because the earlier examination transcript was unavailable through mechanical failure, Presbytery was ordered to reexamine Lutjens, provide a complete transcript, and report by November 10, 1986. Discipline remained conditional on continued nonconformity after pastoral counsel.

1988-08.summary: The complaint was withdrawn after the matter was resolved at a called meeting of Western Carolina Presbytery on June 6, 1988. The published adjudication records no decision on the complaint's merits.

1988-09.title: Morrison et al. v. Philadelphia Presbytery
1988-09.summary: Philadelphia Presbytery treated a letter as a complaint although it had not first been filed with the Session, judged the Session without proper process, and asked its clerk to facilitate membership transfers despite the Session's authority over dismissal letters. Those and a constitutional-limits specification were sustained; claims that Presbytery neglected underlying questions and acted for the Session were not. The March 12 actions were annulled, specified language expunged, and Presbytery directed to adopt safeguards for constitutional inquiries and review relevant church-law materials.

1990-08.summary: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

1990-10.summary: A pastor complained that Presbytery upheld his Session’s refusal to give him financial reports prepared for Session members, while also alleging record-transmission, circularization, factual, and constitutional errors. The SJC denied Specifications 1–5 but sustained Specification 6: because the pastor was a Session member, the Session’s authorization made the reports available to him regardless of whether other elders collected copies. His pastoral relationship had ended, however, so the access claim was moot and conferred no present right to the reports. Reasons for Specifications 1–2 were adopted from Case 90-9.

1991-02.summary: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

1991-06.summary: A member challenged Presbytery’s refusal, after investigation, to try four elders on favoritism charges and its ruling that her related complaint was out of order because dissolution of her church ended her PCA membership. The SJC denied the first item because BCO 31-2 permits declining process when investigation raises no strong presumption of guilt. It sustained the second: jurisdiction properly invoked while a communicant member is not lost through a later status change. No remand was expressly ordered.

1992-01.summary: Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility.

1992-06.summary: After a congregation voted to ask that all ruling elders' official relationships be dissolved without censure, the Session concurred and requested an interim Session. The SJC denied the elders' complaint, holding that BCO 24-6b extends by good and necessary deduction from one elder to multiple identified elders. Dissolution ended their service on that Session but did not divest them of office. Because both the congregation and Session requested it, BCO 13-9 and 15-2 authorized Presbytery to appoint an interim Session. A separate constitutional inquiry was denied without explanation.

1995-10.summary: After Tennessee Valley Presbytery deposed a minister without conducting a church trial, he appealed, alleging denial of PCA due process. The SJC remanded for a new trial. It held that Presbytery could bring charges but could not substitute the Papua New Guinea criminal proceedings for ecclesiastical process, especially when it neither served an indictment and charges nor appointed counsel for an accused unable to attend. The remand permitted a constitutionally compliant trial; it did not resolve guilt or bar discipline.

1995-11.title: James Landrum v. Mississippi Valley Presbytery
1995-11.summary: Complainants challenged Mississippi Valley Presbytery’s approval of James Blaha’s ordination examination, arguing that his views on tongues and prophecy were constitutional exceptions and precluded approval. The SJC agreed that Presbytery should have acknowledged and noted the exceptions, but upheld the examination. It found no proof that Blaha’s denial that the gifts conveyed revelation crossed prior Assembly limits and deferred to Presbytery on an unsettled issue. It expressly declined reexamination or remand; a substantial partial dissent would have set the examination aside.

1997-03.summary: Bruce Nickoley complained against Rocky Mountain Presbytery over its action dissolving the relationship with Evergreen Church. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order under SJC Manual 10.1. The same matter was already the subject of an appeal granted to Evergreen Church and docketed for Presbytery's January 22–24, 1997 meeting, and BCO 43-1 provides that no complaint is allowable in a judicial case in which an appeal is taken. No merits ruling was reached.

1997-04.title: Nancy A. Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
1997-04.summary: After a Session corrected an earlier unauthorized removal from its rolls, then formally voted to remove the same members, the members challenged Presbytery's denial of their complaint, arguing that the new removal defied the prior decision. The SJC upheld Presbytery's action. It concluded that the record showed no unconstitutional procedure or BCO violation and that it could consider only facts properly in the record, not material from earlier cases offered in oral argument. The ruling left the later membership removal undisturbed.

1997-06.summary: After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues.

1997-11.summary: Raymond Larsen sought to appeal a Session judgment deposing him for contumacy after he failed to appear for trial. The SJC unanimously found the appeal administratively out of order because BCO 42-2 permits an appeal only by a person who submitted to a regular trial. The notice does not review the merits of the deposition.

1997-13.summary: New River Presbytery treated Grace Covenant PCA's BCO 41 inquiry about a Sunday school teacher's acceptability as a request for advice, but then ruled he was eligible to teach. On Harvestwood's complaint, the SJC held that Presbytery lacked original jurisdiction to make that final disposition and that the record was unclear about the teacher's views. The SJC sustained the complaint and recommended that Presbytery rescind its March 15, 1997 action and clarify his views through proper BCO procedures; it declined to reach the creation and theistic-evolution merits.

1997-17.summary: A member challenged Presbytery’s approval of a congregational motion supplementing an assistant-pastor fund, alleging that Session had ceded its budget authority. The SJC denied both issues. The motion addressed a special circumstance, not approval of the budget, and left the salary figure to the elders and deacons; Session had already approved the budget and retained control of church funds. The ruling was confined to the congregation’s particular circumstances and did not approve congregational budget adoption.

1998-08.summary: Smith appealed discipline for divisiveness, gossip and slander, broken membership vows, and contumacy arising largely from complaints and letters during church conflict. The SJC sustained her appeal, reversed guilt on all four charges, and annulled suspension from the sacraments. The documentary record proved none of the allegations; filing complaints was not itself divisiveness, and the trial improperly lacked a witness, shifted proof to Smith, showed prejudice, and unfairly rejected her written defense. The SJC declined remand because the evidence was insufficient.

2001-33.summary: A minister challenged Presbytery’s decision to sustain a complaint that rescinded its earlier appellate reversal of a deacon’s conviction and censures. The SJC sustained the minister’s complaint because BCO 43-1 bars a complaint in a judicial case once an appeal has been taken, whether the appeal is past, current, or pending. It reversed Presbytery’s July judgment, restored the April judgment, and remanded to the Session, which could retry the charges using the prior indictment or decline to pursue them.

2001-34.title: Nichols and Couch v. James River Presbytery
2001-34.summary: Church members challenged Presbytery’s repeated delay in granting a properly adopted congregational request to dissolve its pastoral relationship and its gift equivalent to three months of the pastor’s compensation. The SJC found seven complaints judicially out of order, sustained the dissolution-delay challenge, and rejected the gift challenge because Presbytery controlled its own civil property. No further relief was ordered. A concurrence would permit delay based on objective, justifiable findings, but concluded that Presbytery’s stated grounds were insufficient.

2002-01.summary: In a dispute arising from a Korean Eastern Presbytery congregational election, two ruling elders were tried, refused to plead, and were suspended from sacraments and office; KEP denied their appeal, then increased the censures to deposition and excommunication for contumacy. The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The original suspension remained.

2002-02.title: Nichols and Couch v. James River Presbytery
2002-02.summary: Three complaints arising from Presbytery’s treatment of Session actions toward its pastor were judicially out of order. Complaints 10-01 and the unnumbered complaint were filed directly with the SJC without first being presented to James River Presbytery, contrary to BCO 43-2. Complaint 13-01 challenged an action never taken because the motion was ruled out of order. The SJC did not reach their merits. The combined decision’s pastoral-dissolution and benevolent-gift rulings concerned the other consolidated cases, not Case 2002-02.

2002-03.title: Nichols and Couch v. James River Presbytery
2002-03.summary: Ruling elders challenged James River Presbytery’s delay in honoring West End’s valid congregational vote to dissolve its pastoral relationship and a three-month salary gift to the pastor. The SJC held that Presbytery lacked a constitutional basis to delay the dissolution, but rejected the challenge to its benevolent use of its own civil funds. Complaints 16-01, 18-01, and 19-01 were judicially out of order; the others were in order. No remand or repayment was ordered. A concurrence cautioned that prompt dissolution is not automatic when objective, justifiable findings support refusal.

2002-05.summary: A church session suspended a member from the Lord's Table and found her guilty of contumacy. The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

2002-16.summary: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

2003-01.title: Mark Chavalas v. Northern Illinois Presbytery
2003-01.summary: Chavalas appealed a Northern Illinois Presbytery judgment, but testimony cited by both parties was missing from the record. Because recording-machine failures made the required transcripts unavailable and Presbytery could not cure the defect, the SJC found the appeal judicially out of order, dismissed it under SJC Manual 11.6, and suspended Presbytery’s judgment under BCO 42-7. Chavalas’s later resignation did not abandon the appeal because he had appealed beforehand after a regular trial; no rebuke was issued.

2003-02.summary: Thornton challenged Westminster Presbytery’s investigation of TE Frank Smith’s secret recording and its refusal to institute process. The SJC remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation because Presbytery had not timely obtained the other participant’s testimony or examined relevant legal and confessional questions. It rejected claims concerning alleged lying and threats, partiality, and an unbiblical recording policy. The invitation of an outside voluntary prosecutor was moot because he declined; only a separate concurrence found the invitation improper.

2003-03.summary: A minister appealed three convictions and suspension that would automatically become indefinite absent repentance. The SJC sustained the appeal: unauthorized committee citations and admonition without process could not support guilt, and multiple trial violations were fatally prejudicial. It set aside the judgment, dismissed the citation and admonition charges, and revoked both censures. The inappropriate-language charge was not adjudicated on its merits; Presbytery could retry it on remand or dismiss it.

2003-05.summary: Thornton challenged Presbytery’s investigation and refusal to institute process against Smith over secretly recording Roberts, alleged lying and threats, partiality, and its taping policy. The SJC sustained only the challenge to the secret-taping investigation: the committee failed to interview Roberts before reporting and examine the legal and confessional implications of transcription and destruction. It remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation. The other claims lacked sufficient proof; the voluntary-prosecutor issue was moot because Roberts declined.

2003-06.summary: The SJC found Case 2003-6 judicially out of order because the challenged Eastern Carolina Presbytery action was only advice in response to a BCO 41-1 reference from White Oak Session, not a binding or complainable doctrinal decision under BCO 41-3. The underlying dispute—whether elders could hold and teach a broader atonement view—was therefore not reached. The adopted vote was 17 concurring, 1 dissenting, with 1 abstention and 4 absent. The dissent argued Presbytery's 'not allowed' language read as compulsory final disposition.

2004-08.summary: Thornton challenged Westminster Presbytery’s refusal to place Memorial PCA Session’s call in his hands and its simultaneous initiation of administrative divestiture without censure. The SJC sustained both issues, reversed the divestiture decision, and remanded with directions to approve and deliver the call and set an installation date. A valid call supplied the congregational approbation whose absence BCO 34-10’s administrative remedy requires; Presbytery also could not rely on undisclosed concerns while avoiding required judicial process. The ruling found clear error, not an absence of all presbyterial review authority.

2004-12.summary: Mr. M. E. Hunt sought review of an unidentified action by Western Carolina Presbytery. The Assembly record reports that his complaint was found out of order, without identifying an administrative or judicial subtype. It provides no reason, merits determination, relief, or further proceedings.

2005-01.summary: An appeal challenged a presbytery's conviction of a minister for divisive behavior and its indefinite suspension from office and the sacraments. The SJC affirmed: the charge was lawful because publicly publishing disagreement with the session after it acted violated his ordination vows to subjection and peace/unity, even though “divisive” is not a constitutional term; the censure was not unjust absent repentance; procedural errors did not require reversal or remand. A dissent argued the charge failed BCO 29-1’s Scripture-proof requirement.

2005-08.summary: A minister appealed convictions for contumacy and threatening elders with civil litigation, plus deposition and excommunication. The SJC sustained contumacy as failure to remain subject to the brethren under the ordination vow, not BCO 32-6-type contumacy. It sustained deposition but found excommunication excessive given the conflict and replaced it with indefinite suspension from the sacraments. It did not sustain the threat conviction because the attorney’s letter was absent from the record. A dissent disputed the contumacy ruling.

2005-09.summary: A minister challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaints concerning a congregational petition and an Administrative Commission’s actions. The SJC sustained both issues: the petition should first have gone to the Session, and Presbytery and its Commission committed additional constitutional errors. Those errors did not excuse his refusal to obey Presbytery, however. Because he had been deposed in Case 2005-8, further action was moot; the SJC granted no remedy, vacatur, or remand.

2005-12.summary: The 34th General Assembly recorded TE Peter B. Kim’s complaint against Korean Eastern Presbytery as out of order. The sparse published record does not identify the challenged presbytery action, classify the ruling as administrative or judicial, give a rationale, or reach the merits; it specifies no further relief or proceedings.

2006-03.summary: Calvary Presbytery asked that original jurisdiction be assumed concerning S. Wilkins. The 34th General Assembly found the request out of order, but the supplied record gives no reason, merits ruling, relief, or next step. It also does not classify the ruling as administratively or judicially out of order.

2007-01.summary: Lee challenged Korean Eastern Presbytery’s actions affecting his interim pastoral relationship, alleging that its October 3, 2006 meeting lacked a quorum. The SJC held the complaint moot and declared every action taken at that meeting null and void—not merely those concerning his church. The meeting opened with only two ruling elders when three were required, and the minutes did not establish when a quorum was later achieved; its presence therefore could not be presumed.

2007-05.summary: Dr. George W. Mitchell’s appeal against Evangel Presbytery was withdrawn. The 35th General Assembly record reports no merits decision, reason for the withdrawal, or ruling on the unidentified underlying dispute.

2007-08.summary: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

2007-09.summary: Lee challenged Presbytery’s authorization of its Pulpit Commission to act for HKPC’s Session. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled Presbytery’s decision and the Commission’s resulting actions, and directed return of expended church funds if the congregation requested. Neither the Session nor congregation had requested or consented to that authority. The ruling distinguished the Commission’s valid appointment to receive stated-supply requests from its impermissible empowerment to function as the Session or pulpit committee.

2007-10.summary: Lee challenged Korean Eastern Presbytery’s ratification and filing of a New Jersey lawsuit through a commission acting for the local church, seeking civil adjudication of who was the rightful pastor and who could act as the church’s session. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s decision in whole. PCA courts have moral and spiritual, not civil coercive, authority and cannot sue to enforce ecclesiastical decisions. The ruling does not prohibit litigation over purely civil matters and did not condemn the commission’s original appointment.

2007-12.summary: A minister complained that Presbytery placed a shepherding committee report containing findings of his alleged “sins and errors” in its minutes and directed that it be read to his congregation. The SJC sustained the complaint and ordered the report expunged. Although a committee may form and record an opinion without judicial process, Presbytery's endorsement and public dissemination effectively admonished the minister on unsubstantiated and unproven opinions without due process.

2007-16.summary: A minister appealed convictions and indefinite suspension arising from conflict over Presbytery's direction that he resign. The SJC upheld all three convictions, finding two procedural errors nonprejudicial and rejecting the other preserved challenges. But Presbytery could not treat its authority to dissolve a pastoral relationship as authority to compel resignation on pain of discipline. The SJC therefore vacated the censure and dissolution of the call and remanded for reconsideration of censure; Grady's separate administrative suspension remained effective.

2008-07.summary: The complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery was found out of order. The published record does not identify the challenged action, explain the ruling, address the merits, or specify any relief or further proceedings.

2008-08.summary: The 37th General Assembly record reports that DE Joong Min Soh’s complaint against Philadelphia Presbytery was found out of order. It does not identify the challenged action, specify an administrative or judicial subtype, explain the ruling, reach the merits, or record any relief.

2008-15.summary: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

2008-17.summary: Hutchinson and Bulkeley challenged Presbytery’s decision to suspend RE Neill Payne indefinitely from office but not from the Sacraments. The SJC did not sustain the complaint: BCO 30-3 expressly permits suspension from office without sacramental suspension, and no provision requires both censures together. Because the appropriate censure involved discretion and judgment, the SJC deferred absent clear error. Authority to remove or increase Payne’s censure had returned to his Session.

2008-18.summary: Hutchinson and Bulkeley challenged Presbytery’s refusal to condemn RE Neill Payne’s views in a circulated “Africa e-mail.” The SJC did not sustain the complaint. It held that a presbytery may not condemn a church officer’s allegedly erroneous opinions without due process and that four sentences, an approving newspaper reference, and the Commission’s summary did not present Payne’s views fully enough for responsible adjudication. The SJC rejected race or intelligence as the primary determinant of a nation’s fate, while allowing the e-mail to be used as evidence in formal charges.

2009-02.summary: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

2009-03.summary: Leissing challenged Presbytery's November 7 action dissolving the calls of REs Linton and Pellom. By reference to Case 2008-15, the SJC sustained the complaint: the Session had canceled the August 7 congregational meeting, so it generated no valid dissolution request and Presbytery erred in appointing the Sealy Commission. The Commission proceedings, the complaint against its decision, and Presbytery's resulting dissolution action were voided; absent subsequent congregational action, the elders' calls remained undissolved.

2009-08.summary: An elder challenged Presbytery’s failure to interview accusers, alleged investigative delay, and resulting finding of no strong presumption of a pastor’s guilt. The SJC denied the complaint. BCO 31-2 requires due diligence but prescribes no timeline or interview procedure, giving courts substantial discretion before formal process begins. The ordinary stated-meeting sequence used here disclosed no clear constitutional error. The SJC therefore deferred to Presbytery’s superior proximity to the facts and upheld its finding.

2009-09.summary: Lyons challenged Presbytery’s investigation of accusations against a teaching elder, alleging failure to interview accusers, undue delay, and an erroneous finding of no strong presumption of guilt. The SJC denied the complaint and additionally held that Lyons lacked standing because he was not under Presbytery’s jurisdiction. The consolidated opinion explained that BCO 31-2 requires due diligence but prescribes neither interviews nor a timeline; finding no constitutional or clear factual error, it deferred to Presbytery’s judgment.

2009-10.summary: Robert Woodward challenged Presbytery’s acceptance of a finding that accusations against TE Craig Bulkeley did not raise a strong presumption of guilt, alleging investigators never heard his evidence. The SJC denied the complaint, specifically holding that Woodward lacked standing because he was not under Presbytery’s jurisdiction. It also held that BCO 31-2 prescribes no interview requirement or fixed timeline and found no clear constitutional error warranting departure from ordinary deference to Presbytery.

2009-11.title: Larry Edison et al. v. Southwest Florida Presbytery
2009-11.summary: Ministers complained that Southwest Florida Presbytery improperly reexamined Bryan Gregory and reversed his examination, membership, and call after previously receiving him. The SJC upheld Presbytery’s authority to hear and sustain the earlier complaint but sustained the present complaint on the remedial actions. Sustaining a complaint did not itself undo prior acts; once Presbytery had treated Gregory as a member, his membership rights could be removed only through disciplinary due process. The SJC annulled the reexamination and March 24 actions and directed Presbytery to consider appropriate remedies. Gregory’s theology was not before it.

2009-12.summary: Presbytery refused to hear Armes’s complaint against his excommunication, initially reasoning that excommunication deprived him of standing and later ruling the complaint untimely. Presbytery conceded its error on the standing ground, and all parties stipulated to remand for a hearing. The SJC confirmed that stipulation, sustained the complaint, and remanded the case without deciding the validity of the excommunication itself.

2009-13.summary: An unspecified complaint against Southwest Florida Presbytery was found administratively out of order. The published record does not identify the challenged action or explain the administrative defect, and no separate merits opinion, relief, or further proceedings are reported.

2009-16.summary: The published Assembly record reports that Case 2009-16 was found administratively out of order. It does not identify the challenged action, type of proceeding, administrative defect, or any merits ruling or relief; the case therefore supports only that procedural status, not a substantive holding.

2009-21.summary: Armes challenged Presbytery's refusal to hear his second complaint about Session's trespass notice and threat of arrest, which Presbytery treated as duplicating his pending excommunication complaint. The SJC sustained the complaint because the trespass action occurred later and was distinct, although the matters could be heard together. It remanded for Presbytery or a commission to hear the complaint under BCO 43-8. The SJC did not decide whether Session could issue such a notice; review remained subject to timely filing and standing.

2009-24.summary: Phelps complained that Pacific Presbytery erred by finding no constitutional irregularities in the New Life Burbank Session's ordination of Lee Irons as a ruling elder, despite PP's earlier refusal to receive Irons as a teaching-elder candidate. The SJC denied the complaint. Under BCO 39-3.3, the Court owed great deference to the lower court's discretionary fitness judgment; the single office of elder does not require identical eligibility processes, and the NLB Session had jurisdiction after Irons renounced OPC jurisdiction. PP's action stood; the SJC declined to decide the NAPARC issue.

2009-25.summary: Brown challenged Presbytery’s abstract approval of six views concerning diaconal practice. The SJC sustained the consolidated complaints and annulled Presbytery’s action because a church court cannot issue a binding decree apart from properly exercising jurisdiction over specific persons. Constitutional conformity must instead be determined through authorized examination or judicial processes. The judgment deliberately left unresolved whether any of the six views themselves were faithful to the Constitution; the detailed view-by-view analysis appeared only in a concurring opinion.

2009-28.summary: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

2010-16.summary: Kirk Lyons filed BCO 32-2 charges against TE Craig Bulkeley with Western Carolina Presbytery. WCP dismissed the charges, then ruled Lyons's complaint administratively out of order for lack of standing. The SJC answered that the dismissal was not erroneous—Presbytery had discretion under BCO 31-8, 34-2, and 32-20, and the record showed no clear error—but that WCP erred on standing because Lyons's filing brought him under its jurisdiction. Because that error was not prejudicial, the SJC denied the complaint.

2010-17.title: David M. Sarafolean Request to Cite Siouxlands Presbytery
2010-17.summary: TE David M. Sarafolean requested that the General Assembly and SJC cite Siouxlands Presbytery under BCO 40-4 and 40-5. The SJC report records the request as administratively out of order without explaining the defect or deciding the underlying allegations.

2010-18.summary: The SJC considered whether Gulfstream Presbytery had adequately answered a BCO 40-5 citation seeking a more acceptable response to exceptions of substance in its records. It found Gulfstream’s response acceptable, but only pending certification to the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records that the Presbytery had approved it. The decision does not describe the underlying exceptions or give further reasons for finding the response acceptable.

2010-19.summary: Cited under BCO 40-5 to provide a more acceptable response to exceptions of substance in its records, Korean Central Presbytery submitted a response that the SJC accepted, pending certification to the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records that Presbytery had approved it. The ruling accepted the response conditionally; it did not substantively approve the underlying records.

2010-20.summary: Cited under BCO 40-5 for exceptions of substance and failure to submit minutes, Korean Northwest Presbytery provided an acceptable response and submitted its minutes. Acceptance of the substantive response remained contingent on certification that Presbytery had approved it. The minutes were forwarded to the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records, so the ruling established compliance with the citation rather than final approval of the minutes themselves.

2010-21.summary: Korean Southeastern Presbytery was cited under BCO 40-5 for failing to submit its Minutes. The SJC found that Presbytery had since submitted them and directed that they be forwarded to the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records. The decision established compliance with the submission requirement; it did not report substantive exceptions or approve the Minutes on review.

2010-22.summary: Cited under BCO 40-5 for failing to submit its minutes, Korean Southwest Presbytery responded and supplied them. The SJC found that the minutes had been submitted and directed that they be forwarded to the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records. The decision resolved the submission deficiency but left review of the minutes to that committee.

2010-23.summary: Pacific Presbytery was cited under BCO 40-5 to provide a more acceptable response to exceptions of substance found during records review. The SJC accepted its response, conditioned on certification to the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records that Presbytery had approved it. The decision gives no further substantive rationale and, unlike rulings concerning three other presbyteries considered collectively, does not direct that Pacific’s minutes be forwarded.

2010-26.summary: Korean Eastern Presbytery dismissed TE Eliot Lee's charges against two teaching elders without trial, and the SJC sustained Lee's complaint that this was unconstitutional. Although a presbytery may dismiss charges under BCO 29-1, 32-20, 34-2, or 31-8, it bears the burden of documenting that basis; KEP did not. The SJC refused Lee's request that it enter the guilt verdicts the presbytery should have reached—that power exists on appeal, not complaint. It remanded for KEP to begin process under BCO 32.

2010-27.summary: The SJC dismissed Matt Ruff's complaint against Nashville Presbytery as judicially out of order under OMSJC 10.5.a. Ruff challenged Presbytery's failure to investigate a teaching elder, but BCO 43 requires a complaint against an act or decision; lack of action qualifies only when a court meeting has occurred and the court failed to act. Presbytery's nearest antecedent meeting was August 18, 2010, and Ruff filed October 27, 2010, beyond BCO 43-2's thirty-day limit. Because the defect could not be cured, the case was dismissed without reaching the merits; a separate objection disputed that ruling.

2010-28.summary: Gonzales challenged Great Lakes Presbytery’s approval of recommendations following a BCO 31-2 investigation that found no basis for charges. The SJC sustained the complaint only as to recommendation five—which threatened adverse consequences for his recommendation or transfer if he rejected pastoral advice—and annulled its approval. Presbytery could offer pastoral oversight and counsel, including the other recommendations, but without judicial process that counsel could not expressly or implicitly diminish his good standing.

2011-03.summary: Complainants challenged Covenant Presbytery’s receipt and adoption of recommendations from its MNA Committee, alleging that the committee exceeded its assignment to investigate campus-minister salaries. The SJC denied both consolidated complaints. It held that examining Presbytery’s relationship with MJCCW naturally extended the salary inquiry, fell within the committee’s oversight responsibility, and proposed discussion rather than structural change. Presbytery had also ruled the matters properly before it and rejected an appeal. The SJC could not independently verify assertions about the committee’s traditional oversight.

2011-04.summary: Ministers challenged Covenant Presbytery’s receipt of and action on its MNA Committee report concerning the Mississippi Joint Committee on Campus Work, contending that the committee exceeded its assigned authority. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the study naturally extended the salary inquiry, the committee had oversight of MJCCW, the recommendations sought discussion rather than structural change, and Presbytery had ruled the matters properly before it. The record could not establish claimed traditional limits on oversight, and no corrective relief issued.

2011-07.summary: The 39th General Assembly cited Warrior Presbytery under BCO 40 provisions for failing to answer exceptions of substance in several meeting minutes. The SJC recorded that the Presbytery had since submitted responses approved by the Presbytery and found them acceptable. The adopted ruling provides no further rationale or separate relief.

2011-09.summary: North Florida Presbytery restored a minister deposed for adultery by a 19–17 vote. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery had not proceeded with the required caution and that a bare majority could not demonstrate BCO 34-8’s required strongly favorable general sentiment. It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

2011-18.summary: Ruff challenged Nashville Presbytery’s investigation and its resolution of allegations against a minister through confession and admonition without formal process. The SJC sustained the complaint only on the confession and administration of censure: the investigation was adequate and BCO 38-1 was available, but the abstract confession did not acknowledge particular sins against particular people. Presbytery had to amend it, sponsor another reconciliation meeting, document satisfaction with the proceedings, or pursue the matter further, potentially through indictment.

2012-02.summary: Keating challenged Warrior Presbytery’s decision to divest him of ordination without censure while he was absent. The SJC sustained his appeal, reversed and voided the divestiture, and remanded because BCO 34-10’s required opportunity to be heard in his defense was not provided; this also amounted to hurrying before all testimony was taken. It rejected the reasonable-indulgence claim because Presbytery did not know of his postponement request. Keating remained a minister in good standing, but Presbytery could reconsider divestiture after reasonably soliciting a defense.

2012-07.summary: A ruling elder appealed judgments concerning an alleged broken promise to take a sabbatical and deficient performance as Session clerk. Because the pivotal email was absent from the record, the SJC vacated the sabbatical-related judgment and remanded for Presbytery only to consider whether a new trial was warranted. It reversed and dismissed the clerk-duty specification because the four-month delay in submitting minutes was attributable to the Session and did not justify a trial. Only the first specification remained potentially triable.

2012-08.title: Art Sartorius et al. v. Siouxlands Presbytery
2012-08.summary: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

2013-04.summary: Hope Community Church’s Session challenged Presbytery’s requirement that a multi-site congregation eventually particularize its second worship site. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled the requirement, and struck it from the Presbytery Manual because BCO 12-5e specifically entrusts the time and place of worship to the Session, which Presbytery’s general church-enlargement authority could not supersede. The narrow ruling did not resolve broader concerns about multi-site churches or eliminate Presbytery’s review of a second site’s location under BCO 13-9(g).

2013-06.summary: A minister appealed Great Lakes Presbytery’s divestiture of his office without censure under BCO 34-10. The SJC sustained his claim that Presbytery failed to make required findings that he habitually neglected official functions and that any neglect arose only from lack of acceptance to the Church. It reversed and annulled the divestiture, leaving him a member in good standing, and required no further action. The other four specifications were moot. Presbytery remained free to pursue proper Chapter 31 process or a procedurally compliant BCO 34-10 divestiture.

2013-08.summary: Jackson challenged Northwest Georgia Presbytery’s failure to act on his BCO 40-5 letter alleging delinquency by Midway’s Session. The SJC found his complaint administratively out of order and dismissed it because he was not a commissioner at Presbytery’s January 2013 meeting; originating a BCO 40-5 report did not confer standing. Separately, the SJC accepted jurisdiction over Presbytery’s failure to respond and remitted the matter for constitutional disposition, without deciding whether the Session committed the alleged delinquencies.

2013-11.summary: A Session appealed Presbytery’s judgment finding it guilty and suspending it for refusing instructions to institute process against a member. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed the judgment in whole, and dismissed the charges. Once Presbytery denied the member’s complaint, that matter should have ended; moreover, Presbytery did not follow BCO 40-4’s required first step before invoking BCO 40-5 review and control. The delay, prejudice, and missing-witness specifications were moot. The decision did not fault Presbytery’s underlying concern.

2015-04.summary: Thompson used a BCO 43 complaint to challenge his Session indictment during an ongoing disciplinary case, according to the separate concurrence. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order. It held that a defendant must raise such objections during process in the court of original jurisdiction under BCO 32-14 and, if still dissatisfied, pursue them on appeal under BCO 42-3. The ruling did not decide the indictment objection’s merits.

2015-05.summary: A BCO 40-5 application to cite Granada Presbyterian Church for alleged grossly unconstitutional proceedings and discipline delinquencies was found administratively out of order and dismissed as prematurely filed. The SJC held that, even assuming a credible report, BCO 40-5 first required citing the offending court before South Florida Presbytery, the court of appellate jurisdiction. Because Presbytery had docketed the matter for its August 11, 2015 meeting and had not yet ruled, the SJC could not act. No merits ruling on the discipline allegations was made.

2015-06.summary: Reviewing South Florida Presbytery’s response to a General Assembly citation, the SJC found most responses satisfactory but rejected one because it did not address BCO 32-2’s requirement to proceed once a charge is made. It approved previously unsubmitted 2009 executive-session minutes with an exception because their treatment of a teaching elder appeared to violate BCO 46-8. Presbytery also had to submit amended minutes and complete, or formally plan, overdue Session-record reviews for report to the 45th General Assembly.

2015-10.summary: The SJC dismissed a BCO 40-5 application because the matter concerned proceedings in a judicial case in which a complaint had been filed. Under BCO 40-3, such proceedings may not be handled by review and control once notice of appeal or complaint is given to the lower court. The SJC therefore found the case administratively out of order and not capable of being put in order under OMSJC 9.1.a., and dismissed it under OMSJC 9.2(d).

2015-11.summary: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

2016-01.summary: An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. A concurrence believed the SJC could also have adjudicated the confessional-difference merits; a dissent would have found noncompliance and reached the merits.

2016-09.summary: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

2016-11.summary: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

2017-03.summary: The 46th General Assembly record listed Daniels et al.’s complaint against Nashville Presbytery as out of order. The sparse published record does not identify the challenged action, specify an administrative or judicial subtype, provide a reason, or decide the merits.

2017-04.summary: The 2017-04 BCO 40-5 report of RE John B. Thompson was withdrawn in the 46th General Assembly (2018) record, and no separate merits opinion was published. The available record states no underlying facts, issues, adopted reasons, or relief; it supplies only the docket disposition of the report.

2017-06.summary: Blue Ridge Presbytery asked the SJC to hear and decide a complaint by reference. The SJC denied the request because the record demonstrated neither presbytery-wide disqualification nor serious division, constitutional questions, or new, delicate, or difficult issues warranting reference. Presbytery therefore had to hear and decide the complaint itself. The ruling concerned only the proper court for adjudication and did not decide the complaint’s merits; companion case 2017-07 was answered by reference to this decision.

2017-07.summary: Blue Ridge Presbytery sought to have the SJC decide Clements’s complaint rather than hear it locally. Answering the complaint by reference to companion case 2017-06, the SJC directed Presbytery to hear and decide it because the record did not establish bias, serious division, constitutional questions, or unusually difficult issues warranting reference under BCO 41. The ruling did not decide the complaint’s merits.

2017-09.title: BCO 40-5 Report of RE John B. Thompson
2017-09.summary: The 46th General Assembly ruled the BCO 40-5 report of RE John B. Thompson out of order. The published record does not describe the report’s allegations, specify an administrative or judicial subtype, or provide reasons or a separate merits opinion.

2018-03.summary: The SJC considered whether it could receive directly a BCO 31-2 report affecting Christian character. It ruled the matter administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order because no constitutional provision authorizes such direct receipt. The order did not address the report’s substance or direct further proceedings.

2019-03.summary: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

2019-05.summary: An excommunicated member appealed the Missouri Presbytery judicial commission's guilty verdict and excommunication, alleging specifications of error. The SJC denied the appeal and did not sustain any specification, holding only that the appellant failed to demonstrate sufficient reason to sustain the alleged errors; the excommunication thus remained in effect. The record noted Presbytery dismissed the commission without the BCO 15-3 vote to approve its report, but the adopted reasoning gave no further explanation and did not address that fact.

2019-06.summary: In a BCO 40-5 matter, the SJC held that a presbytery erred in upholding a session's erasure of a member who pled not guilty to failing to submit and pursued divorce. The session wrongly equated declining divorce counsel with refusing submission, failed to assess membership duties in another branch, failed to notify her of erasure, and proceeded without process after dropping charges. The SJC sustained the challenge, directed the session to note the notice failure and remove her under BCO 38-3(a), but ordered no express reversal.

2019-08.summary: A minister appealed a judgment finding him guilty on most charges and imposing six months’ suspension. The SJC held BCO 32-20 barred Specifications 1, 2, and 4 because Presbytery lacked extraordinary justification for prosecuting old allegations, but did not bar ongoing Specification 3. It separately found the entire process constitutionally flawed and prejudicial. The SJC reversed the whole censure, declined Presbytery’s requested harsher sentence, and concluded the matter. A concurrence disputed the majority’s BCO 32-20 interpretation while agreeing with the result.

2019-10.summary: Arizona Presbytery deposed TE John Evans without process after considering investigative-committee observations he had not approved. The SJC sustained the joined complaints, annulled the deposition, and remanded. BCO 38-1 requires the accused and court to approve one full statement of facts; Evans could not approve facts presented after he left. But the provision does not expressly require a meeting or detailed discussion. The underlying matter remained unresolved: Presbytery could proceed with or without process, or dismiss it.

2019-13.summary: A member removed from the rolls under BCO 38-4 challenged Presbytery's ruling that she lacked standing to complain because she was no longer a member. The SJC sustained the complaint: standing under BCO 43-1 cannot be defeated by the very removal challenged. Removal under BCO 38-4 is pastoral discipline, a disciplinary case, not a merely administrative act. The SJC remanded to Presbytery to consider the complaint and take the action it should have taken—remand to the Session. The merits of the removal were not decided.

2020-06.summary: A church member appealed Presbytery’s affirmance of his conviction and excommunication for failing to heed Session admonition and membership vows, including prolonged absence from that church. The SJC affirmed and denied the appeal, holding that all four specifications—lack of reasonable indulgence, haste, prejudice, and injustice—were nonspecific and unsupported. It emphasized his admissions that the charges were true, the adequate timeline, and the bar on considering evidence not offered at trial. A dissent disputed his PCA membership, standing, and the Session’s jurisdiction.

2020-07.summary: Pacific Presbytery allowed its Judicial Commission to read a six-page adverse report containing new assertions beyond TE Rankin Wilbourne's agreed BCO 38-1 confession, then ruled his sins "base and flagitious" and deposed him. The SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the deposition, holding BCO 38-1 barred the prejudicial report and BCO 34-7 did not apply without a pending trial. It recommended treating the 17-month censure as sufficient definite suspension, restoring ministerial standing without call, and closing the matter; dissolution of his call was not annulled.

2020-09.title: Sean Ozbalt and Erin Barr v. Pacific Presbytery
2020-09.summary: Pacific Crossroads Church’s Session challenged Presbytery’s handling of a minister’s BCO 38-1 confession, particularly its hearing an adverse investigative report outside the agreed statement before imposing deposition. The SJC sustained Case 2020-09 by reference to its consolidated decision and annulled the deposition: BCO 38-1 permits censure to rest only on the mutually approved statement, not additional adverse material. It recommended treating the elapsed 17 months as definite suspension and closing the matter. The minister returned to good standing without call; dissolution of his call remained intact.

2020-11.summary: The complaint against Southwest Florida Presbytery ended when the SJC approved Complainant David McWilliams's request to withdraw and abandon it, by unanimous roll-call vote (24-0-0) on March 25, 2021. The adopted decision recites no underlying dispute, merits analysis, or reasons and makes no substantive ruling; the complaint stands withdrawn and abandoned. The sparse record is useful only as an example of an approved pre-decision withdrawal/abandonment.

2021-02.summary: In this BCO 40-5 request, the SJC advised the Stated Clerk that Tippins v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery should be referred to the General Assembly's Review of Presbytery Records Committee. The SJC approved that action 19-3-0; three commissioners dissented. The sparse record supplies no underlying facts, merits analysis, or reason for the referral.

2021-03.summary: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

2021-06.summary: Herron and others challenged Presbytery’s decision to proceed to trial after a BCO 31-2 finding, his administrative suspension, denial of access to Presbytery records and meetings, and a public statement. The SJC sustained only the access issue: suspension from official functions did not remove his membership rights, though it did not entitle him to every investigative-committee document. Finding no clear error on the other issues, it ordered trial to proceed, temporarily stayed censure decisions, and postponed related complaints through trial and any appeal.

2021-11.summary: Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s action because discipline preceded particular charges and a specific confession, and because an independent church lacked authority to impose PCA censure. It declared the underlying matter moot because the alleged event was twenty-one years old and the victim would not cooperate, ending the proceeding without remand. The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically.

2021-13.summary: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

2021-14.summary: Herron challenged Presbytery's handling of its directive that he withdraw his civil defamation lawsuit. The SJC answered the complaint by reference to its completed trial decision in 2022-10, which acquitted him on all seven charges, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to ministerial good standing. The incorporated decision found the lawsuit's sinfulness unproved; the complaint notice supplied no separate issue-by-issue ruling.

2021-15.summary: Barber and others challenged Presbytery's actions rescinding Herron's contumacy judgment. The SJC answered their complaint by reference to its completed trial decision in 2022-10, which acquitted Herron on all seven charges, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to ministerial good standing. That decision found the lawsuit's sinfulness unproved, undermining the related contumacy charge. The complaint notice supplied no separate issue-by-issue ruling.

2022-02.summary: The SJC answered this Herron-related complaint by reference to its final decision in the Herron trial, which acquitted him on all seven charges, removed all censures and administrative suspensions imposed by Presbytery, and restored his good standing as a minister. The complaint notice supplies no separate ruling on its individual allegations.

2022-20.summary: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.
