2022-21.summary: A minister challenged Presbytery’s procedures and its classification of a transfer candidate’s views on continuing tongues as “not a difference.” The SJC rejected the procedural objections because Presbytery could disregard its committee’s recommendation and had breached no required procedure. It nevertheless held that a difference need not overtly contradict the Standards and that the candidate’s statements implicated WCF 1.1 and 1.6. It annulled the classification and remanded for clarification and a new judgment, without deciding whether the clarified view would be acceptable.

2023-04.summary: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

2023-07.summary: Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the divestiture because BCO 38-3(a) had already ended Presbytery's jurisdiction while he was in good standing and under no investigation or charges. It directed Presbytery to record the irregular withdrawal, acknowledge his new membership, and remove him from its roll.

2023-10.summary: Elders challenged Presbytery’s authority and vague instruction for its Shepherding Committee to “follow up” with their Session. The SJC denied the constitutional challenge because the record reasonably supported concern for the church’s peace and spiritual welfare, but sustained the challenge to Presbytery’s lack of specific direction and poor communication. The decision distinguishes prohibited mandatory visitation without cause from a reasonably justified visit, while requiring clarity about its objectives. It did not decide the underlying doxology dispute or order further relief.

2023-11.summary: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

2023-13.summary: A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery's failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord's Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church's session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly's direct referral but did not void it.

2023-19.summary: A filing challenging Presbytery’s handling of Huffman’s BCO 38-1 confession was styled as an appeal under a newly amended rule. The SJC found it judicially out of order because the case began and was nearly completed when the former rule provided review by complaint, and retroactive application would be unfair. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the filing as a complaint at its next stated meeting; denial or failure to act permits review by the SJC. No merits issue was decided.

1976-02.summary: Trinity Church complained that Grace Presbytery's July 9, 1976 substitute motion, delaying Adrian Pater's ordination until he was called to PCA work, was an out-of-order reconsideration. The Judicial Commission did not reach the merits: because the BCO 43-5 record was not complied with and minutes were inadequate, it returned the whole matter to the lower court for a new hearing. The Assembly accepted that judgment and separately adopted, 238–131, a recommendation that the BCO does not envisage ordination expressly for pastoral service in another denomination.

1981-03.summary: A complaint challenged Presbytery's one-year delay before accepting a petition to organize a mission congregation. The General Assembly adopted the Judicial Commission's report and did not sustain the complaint. It reasoned BCO 5-1(1) gives Presbytery discretion over the time for organization, the group had sought only mission status, and the dispute was best handled at Presbytery, where complainants could seek reconsideration. A dissent recommending sustain and annulment was admitted but not adopted.

1982-02.summary: A teaching elder complained that Central Georgia Presbytery wrongly refused to sustain his complaint against a session that closed a disciplinary matter involving unbiblical separation, divorce, and remarriage before any judicial action. The General Assembly's Judicial Commission sustained the complaint, treating the session's "closing of the matter" as the central issue. It did not grant the requested reproof, suspension, or excommunication; it requested the presbytery to aid the session in corrections and heed WCF 24:6 and SC 87 on divorce and repentance.

1984-01.summary: A ruling elder complained that Central Carolina Presbytery violated the BCO in examining and approving Rick Downs for ordination, citing five specifications about the call, Downs’s Sabbath exception, the revote after an initial disapproval, lack of Scriptural search, and ordination questions. The judicial commission held points 1, 2, 4, and 5 not sustained 11–0 and point 3 not sustained 10–1; the general complaint was not sustained 11–0, and the lower court decision was confirmed. Its explanatory opinion said the commission disagreed on the Sabbath/subscription question and acted largely because the specifications did not substantiate the complaint.

1984-02.summary: Central Florida Presbytery received a minister while he had a pending call to labor in another presbytery. A Judicial Commission sustained the specification of error, holding that BCO 13-2,5 barred receiving him under those circumstances; the vote was 9–4. It also voted 13–0 to remand the entire matter for proper procedures regarding his admission to the PCA. The Commission commended the presbytery's aim of receiving him but ruled the process erroneous, leaving the admission to be handled through proper procedures.

1984-06.summary: A complaint challenged North Georgia Presbytery's transfer of Trinity Mission, Elberton, Georgia, to Central Georgia Presbytery, alleging insufficient debate and failure to examine discipline issues. The Judicial Commission unanimously did not sustain the specification of error. Its adopted explanation found that two years of contact and discussions had done as much as possible to clear misunderstanding. It nevertheless noted the presbytery's inadequate explanation and the complainants' failure to secure adequate information; no relief was granted, and the listed questions about congregational choice and transfer power were not answered.

1985-05.summary: Can a presbytery require an annual committee visit to every session and congregation absent a request or evident problem? The judicial commission sustained the complaint against Missouri Presbytery 16-0, holding BCO 11-4 limits higher-court jurisdiction to express constitutional provisions and BCO 13-9 contains no clear authorization for such required visits. It instructed presbytery to conform its Standing Rules and visitation procedures to the BCO, while encouraging voluntary pastoral oversight; several commissioners recorded negative votes without stated reasons.

1986-02.summary: A complaint challenged Grace Presbytery's approval and installation of a candidate who had been divorced for his own infidelity and had remarried; the complainants argued Scripture, the Westminster Confession, BCO 16-3, and the Seventh General Assembly's divorce report barred ordination. The Judicial Commission did not sustain any of the four specifications and upheld Presbytery's action. Its adopted reason was that the PCA's constitutional statements do not explicitly address divorce and remarriage for church officers; noting wide interpretive disagreement, it called for study. The ordination and installation remained undisturbed.

1986-04.summary: An appeal challenged Great Lakes Presbytery's decision to divest TE Edward A. Steele III without censure and without judicial process, which he alleged followed an accusation that he was not engaged in his official duties. Steele alleged constitutional and discriminatory error and sought investigation, rescission, or erasure of his name. Because no one appeared to represent the appeal, the Committee on Judicial Business judged it abandoned, leaving the merits and requested relief undecided.

1987-01.summary: Philadelphia Presbytery ordained Lester Porter as a Ruling Elder of Presbytery to serve a cross-cultural mission church with no particular-church members. The Assembly, adopting the Judicial Commission's adjudication, sustained all three specifications and upheld the complaint: the ordination lacked BCO compliance and the Presbytery mishandled the complaint. It refused to annul Porter's ordination—reasoning Presbytery may ordain Ruling Elders in organizing churches—but directed Presbytery to find a BCO-conforming temporary government for Church Without Walls, stop ordaining Ruling Elders not duly elected by a particular church, and bring Porter's ordination into conformity.

1988-03.summary: Complainant elders challenged Philadelphia Presbytery's tie-vote refusal to sustain its judicial commission's judgment that the Calvary Session wrongly treated physical cruelty as biblical grounds for divorce. The General Assembly adopted the commission's judgment sustaining all three specifications: the Session's action contravened Matthew 5 and 19, WCF 24:6, and the church's disciplinary role. It annulled Presbytery's refusal and instructed Presbytery to advise the Session that physical cruelty is not biblical or confessional grounds for divorce. The explanatory opinion urged pastoral alternatives, such as separation and rehabilitation, before any divorce determination.

1988-05.summary: Missouri Presbytery instructed its Candidates and Credentials Committee to examine candidates without treating a qualified minority view on prophecy and tongues as disqualifying. Complainants argued this conflicted with the 1986 Gentry decision. The Judicial Commission, adopted by the 16th General Assembly, did not sustain the complaint and confirmed the lower court 7-4. Although earlier similar cases had annulled lower-court actions, it cited the absence of a specific candidate, safeguards, inconclusive debate, and a preference for grass-roots resolution, encouraging Overture 25. The dissent called the view fundamentally out of accord.

1988-07.summary: A ruling elder complained that Western Carolina Presbytery wrongly left a confessing bisexual Teaching Elder under indefinite suspension rather than deposing him, excluding him from the sacraments, and cutting him off from fellowship. The General Assembly's adjudicating commission did not sustain the specification of error and confirmed Presbytery's action, holding it complied with BCO 30-3, 4 and 34-7. Review was limited to the constitutionality of the disciplinary process; the commission cited Presbytery's restorative purpose and evidence of repentance. The Assembly was advised Presbytery later deposed the Teaching Elder.

1988-10.summary: The 16th General Assembly approved the adjudicating Commission’s judgment sustaining a complaint against Palmetto Presbytery. The Commission found that Presbytery erred by sustaining John Tomlinson’s theology examination and licensing him despite his belief in continuing noncanonical revelation through prophecy, tongues, dreams, visions, and direct speech, contrary to WCF I.1 and I.6 and BCO 7-1. It directed Presbytery to annul the theology examination, suspend its licensing action, counsel and re-examine Tomlinson, exercise greater care, and report to the next Assembly.

1992-02.summary: A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.'s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

1992-09b.summary: Overman carried to the General Assembly his complaint that Eastern Carolina Presbytery improperly licensed Arthur Peterson, after the presbytery denied it. The SJC found the complaint not in order for lack of standing: Overman was not subject to the presbytery's jurisdiction (BCO 43-1; MSJC 6.2). It made no merits ruling; the same basic issue was noted as pending in a complaint by the Antioch Presbyterian Church session. The source header labels the disposition 'dismissed.'

1993-01.summary: Smith complained that Northeast Presbytery failed to provide pastoral care after dissolving Grace Presbyterian Church. The SJC rejected Presbytery's objections that the complaint lacked supporting reasons or was barred by Smith's protest, held it in order, but denied it on the merits. Distinguishing the pastoral 'power of order' from judicial 'power of jurisdiction,' the SJC ruled that the Constitution neither requires nor permits a presbytery to retain jurisdiction over individual members of a dissolved particular church, and that pastoral care of former members is generally discretionary; on these facts, Presbytery's efforts satisfied any duty.

1993-02.summary: An appeal challenged Evangel Presbytery's judgment that a teaching elder wrongfully pursued divorce without biblical grounds, alleging procedural irregularities, refused evidence, haste, prejudice, and mistaken censure. The SJC rejected each claim: failure to swear two minor witnesses was acknowledged and nonprejudicial, notices and defense opportunity were adequate, and the guilty finding rested on Scripture, WCF 24:6, BCO 26-1, and 30-3; the 1992 study did not authorize divorce for alleged spiritual desertion. The appeal was not sustained, leaving the indefinite suspension in force; one commissioner dissented.

1996-06.summary: The Standing Judicial Commission approved the panel's action dismissing Robert Williams's complaint against South Texas Presbytery as judicially out of order. The adopted reason was that the parties could not agree on the Record of the Case. The source does not describe the challenged Presbytery action, the complaint's specifications, or any merits ruling.

1997-02.summary: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

1997-08.summary: Whether a non-PCA church member may bring a complaint against a presbytery? The full Standing Judicial Commission held no, finding Theresa Bridie's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery judicially out of order because she was not a member of a PCA church and therefore lacked standing. No merits issue was reached, and the sparse record does not identify the challenged presbytery action.

1997-10.summary: Raymond Larsen's complaint against Pacific Presbytery (Case 97-10) was withdrawn by the complainant before any merits ruling, and the Assembly recorded that withdrawal at its next stated meeting. His companion Case 97-12, also against Pacific Presbytery, was withdrawn at the same time. No separate merits opinion was published, so the record supplies only the disposition and no reasons, facts, or relief.

1998-01.summary: The complaint challenged James River Presbytery's approval of an ordination examination in which the candidate called the Genesis creation days God's anthropomorphic work days, not necessarily twenty-four-hour days. The complainant argued that view conflicted with WCF I.9. The SJC denied the complaint and answered 'No' to whether the Presbytery erred; the examination stood. It held the Presbytery had authority and discretion, no General Assembly had declared anthropomorphic days contrary to the Standards, and an advisory-committee study left the SJC unwilling to decide creation-day length. A six-member dissent sought an exception and study-committee referral.

1998-02.summary: The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.

1998-05.summary: At issue was whether James River Presbytery erred by instructing TE Andrew Conrad not to teach or preach his views that the Genesis days were not necessarily six twenty-four-hour days, after JRP treated the views as an exception. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving JRP's instruction in effect. It deferred under BCO 39-3, finding no significant procedural or constitutional error and no clear error of discretion; the parties had stipulated that instruction as the sole issue. The eight dissenters would have found JRP exceeded its discretion.

1998-09.summary: An appeal from a Presbytery judgment and indefinite suspension of a pastor turned on whether he violated the Ninth Commandment and ordination/installation vows by telling the congregation the Session had 'demanded' his resignation for six weeks. The SJC denied the appeal, holding the Session as a whole had not formally demanded resignation; individual elders' earlier opinions did not excuse the overstatement, which harmed the Session's good name. It also found no due-process irregularity or prejudice warranting reversal, deferring to the lower court under BCO 39-3, leaving indefinite suspension in place.

1998-10.summary: Eastern Carolina Presbytery referred to the SJC both TE Byron Curtis's complaint against Presbytery's order barring him from teaching his exceptions and TE Jeff Black's already-sustained complaint on the same subject. Without reaching the merits, the SJC remanded to the Presbytery for adjudication at the next stated meeting, directing that Curtis's complaint be heard. It reasoned that judicial complaints in process cannot be referred for mere advice and that, despite uncertainty about what the Presbytery sought, the lower court should hear the case first. Five SJC members dissented; the merits remained open.

1999-02.summary: Tan's complaint challenged South Texas Presbytery's action at its July 30–31, 1999 meeting. The SJC declared the complaint administratively out of order because it was untimely under BCO 43-3: although dated and faxed August 28, it was not mailed until September 4 and was received September 7—beyond 30 days. SJC Manual 19.10 requires receipt in the Stated Clerk's office and disallows fax filing. The merits were not reached. Twenty-two members concurred; one was recused and one absent.

1999-05.summary: After a minister remained on his presbytery's rolls without call and outside its bounds for more than seven years, the presbytery completed involuntary divestiture without censure. He appealed. The SJC denied the appeal and sustained the divestiture, reasoning that BCO 13-2 and 34-10 allowed the presbytery to follow that procedure once the constitutional three-year limit had long passed and no call to a particular ministry was available. The action therefore left the divestiture without censure in force.

2000-02.summary: A prosecutor's complaint relating to Northeast Presbytery's judicial case was held administratively out of order by the SJC. The SJC adopted two grounds: BCO 43-1 bars a complaint about a matter subject to an appeal in another case, and the complaint sought retrial of an accused on charges of which he had been acquitted, relief the SJC could not grant. Although the related appeal was later withdrawn and the withdrawal approved, the SJC still applied BCO 43-1. A concurrence disputed that first ground and urged BCO clarification of appellate review of acquittals. No merits ruling was made.

2000-04.summary: The SJC found a complaint against North Texas Presbytery out of order because the complainant lacked standing: he was not a member of a PCA church. It did not reach the merits or identify the underlying presbytery action. The vote was 19 concur, 0 dissent, 0 abstain, and 5 absent. The sparse minute entry illustrates that complaint standing before the SJC requires PCA membership; no separate reasoning or incorporated decision appears.

2000-10.summary: The SJC found Roger Tinsley et al.'s complaint against Southeast Alabama Presbytery out of order because it was not timely filed within BCO 43-3's 30-day limit following the lower court's meeting. It therefore reached no merits and granted no relief. The sparse record does not describe the challenged presbytery action. Vote: 14 concur, 0 dissent, 0 abstain, 9 absent, 1 recused.

2001-02.summary: Korean Capital Presbytery's commission tried and suspended a Korean church assistant pastor for heresy and schism after he failed to answer two summonses, and Presbytery upheld the suspension. On appeal, the SJC sustained the procedural challenge because no indictment with witnesses had been served and the record lacked any minutes or hearing for the default judgment, contrary to BCO 32-3. The SJC remanded for a new trial but expressly declined to rule on the citations, default procedure, or merits.

2001-06.summary: The SJC sustained a complaint by two ruling elders against Korean Eastern Presbytery over a disputed congregational meeting (three commissioners dissented). The session was deadlocked and had not called a requested meeting; KEP's administrative commission called and supervised the February 18, 2001 meeting, and KEP approved that action. The SJC reversed both lower-court actions, holding that BCO 25-2 places responsibility on the session and that the presbytery's proper course was to adjudicate a complaint under BCO 43, not act for the session. It declined to rule on the meeting's legal effect.

2001-11.title: Byung Han Yoo v. Korean Northwest Presbytery
2001-11.summary: A ruling elder's complaint against Korean Northwest Presbytery was found out of order because it was untimely under BCO 43-2. The action complained of was taken October 10, 2000, but the complaint was filed March 12, 2001, well outside the 30-day filing period, so the SJC reached no merits question. The case illustrates that a complaint failing BCO 43-2 timeliness is dismissed without adjudication of the underlying presbytery action.

2001-13.title: Samuel Hong v. Korean Capital Presbytery
2001-13.summary: Deacon Samuel Hong appealed after Korean Capital Presbytery's special judicial commission convicted him of contumacy and making a false statement and imposed a two-year suspension from the sacraments. The SJC sustained the appeal, holding that original jurisdiction over charges against a communicant member belongs to the local Session, not Presbytery or its commission, and reversed the Presbytery/commission actions. The SJC did not decide the underlying charges; the reversal was jurisdictional, not an acquittal. One recorded dissent gave no reasons.

2001-15.title: In Mo Chung v. Korean Capital Presbytery
2001-15.summary: The SJC decided whether a presbytery and its special judicial commission could assume original jurisdiction over disciplinary charges against a church member. It sustained the appeal and reversed: the court of original jurisdiction for communicant members is the local church session. Because the appellant was a member of Korean Presbyterian Church of Washington, the presbytery and its commission acted contrary to constitutional standards when they adjudicated the charges and imposed excommunication. The ruling rested on jurisdiction, not the merits; no remand was ordered.

2001-16.title: Joo Bok Suh v. Korean Capital Presbytery
2001-16.summary: In this SJC appeal, RE Joo Bok Suh challenged Korean Capital Presbytery's excommunication after its special judicial commission, rather than his local session, received and adjudicated charges that he had committed contumacy and made a false statement in a civil-court filing. The SJC sustained the appeal and reversed the Presbytery/commission action because the court of original jurisdiction over a communicant member is the local session. The reversal was jurisdictional; the SJC did not rule on the truth of the charges, so it was not an acquittal.

2001-17.title: Choon Soon Lee v. Korean Capital Presbytery
2001-17.summary: Korean Capital Presbytery approved a three-year suspension from the sacraments after its special judicial commission found RE Choon Soon Lee guilty of contumacy and making a false statement on a civil-court document. On appeal, the SJC sustained and reversed. Because Lee was a communicant member, the Session—not Presbytery or its commission—was the court of original jurisdiction; the commission's adjudication therefore violated constitutional standards. The SJC did not decide the underlying charges, and one commissioner dissented.

2001-18.title: Sang Soo Ryoo v. Korean Capital Presbytery
2001-18.summary: The SJC sustained an assistant pastor’s appeal from a three-year suspension from the sacraments after a Korean Capital Presbytery commission found him guilty of participating in the call of an allegedly unconstitutional presbytery meeting. The decisive defect was procedural: no indictment was served, no prosecutor was clearly appointed, and no trial minutes appeared in the record; service of an indictment with a witness list was critical. The case was remanded for a new trial, and the SJC expressly did not reach the merits or citation adequacy.

2001-24.title: Keith A. Williams v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
2001-24.summary: A complaint by Keith A. Williams against Eastern Carolina Presbytery was withdrawn. The 30th Assembly's 2002 record lists it among withdrawn cases, and the stub identifies the Standing Judicial Commission as the court. No separate merits opinion was published; the source does not describe the challenged presbytery action, any issue-level ruling, or any adopted reason. The only usable information is the procedural disposition.

2001-25.title: Anthony Dallison v. North Florida Presbytery
2001-25.summary: After TE Anthony Dallison confessed spousal abuse and received an indefinite suspension, North Florida Presbytery later found him impenitent and deposed him and suspended him from the sacraments. Dallison complained that increasing the censure required fresh charges and trial. The SJC disagreed: his BCO 38-1 confession waived trial rights as to the original charge; the offender then had to satisfy the court of repentance, and the presbytery could investigate and impose higher censure under BCO 37-3, 37-4, 37-8, and 34-4b. The complaint was not sustained.

2001-28.title: Larry Ball v. Westminster Presbytery
2001-28.summary: A complaint challenged Westminster Presbytery's denial of a challenge to its May 15, 2001 plan to withdraw from the PCA. The SJC answered no: the Presbytery did not err, and denied the complaint. BCO 25's local-church withdrawal right and the BCO Preface's grassroots principles extend to presbyteries unless expressly excluded, so a presbytery may determine its own membership and affiliation. The plan did not 'act for' local churches; they retained rights to remain in the PCA or leave, and retained property and internal operations.

2001-30.summary: Third Presbyterian Church asked the SJC to review Evangel Presbytery's denial of its complaint against a Presbytery commission's binding arbitration award of $57,000 to Covenant Classical School. The SJC ruled the complaint not judicially in order, not denied on the merits: PCA courts may not serve as civil arbitrators, and neither Presbytery nor the SJC may review legally binding arbitration judgments. Church courts may act only as ecclesiastical arbitrators, whose decisions lack civil effect and are reviewable under BCO 43. The complaint's five grounds were not reached.

2001-31.summary: After Deacon Neil Jeansonne was convicted by his Session of causing dissension and strife, Eastern Carolina Presbytery reversed, then reinstated the conviction; the SJC asked whether his General Assembly appeal was properly before it. It was not. Because Case 2001-33 held ECP erred in hearing RE Williams's complaint, ECP's April 21, 2001 reversal and removal of censures stand. The case is remanded to the Session, which may retry using the prior indictment or not pursue the matter. BCO 43-1 barred the complaint once appeal was taken.

2001-32.summary: Christ Covenant Church Session complained under BCO 43 that Central Carolina Presbytery wrongly annulled the session trial commission's judgment and found due-process error concerning H. The SJC did not reach the merits. It held the case not judicially in order because H's complaint to the Session was untimely: it exceeded the thirty-day requirement of BCO 43-2 and came more than eighty days after the oral verdict. The ruling thus turned on a procedural gate, making no merits ruling on Presbytery's annulment or its due-process rationale.

2002-09.summary: The SJC denied TE Stuart H. Merriam's appeal from Tennessee Valley Presbytery's April 20, 2002 conviction on three ordination-vow specifications and its indefinite suspension. It rejected procedural challenges—that the earlier called meeting was improperly convened and that TVP was prejudiced by prior cases—and found no clear error, applying BCO 39-3(2)'s deference to lower-court factual findings. The SJC sustained TVP's judgment; prior SJC Cases 95-10 and 96-7 had only indirect bearing and did not require retrial.

2002-10.summary: A church member challenged Pacific Northwest Presbytery's denial of her complaint that Faith Presbyterian Church (Tacoma) Session had banned her from worship and sought to erase her membership retroactively under BCO 38-4. The SJC sustained the complaint. Because she never joined Covenant PCA, BCO 46-3 left her membership under Faith's Session; the Session's proposed retroactive erasure did not comply with BCO 38-4's pastoral-oversight steps. The Presbytery therefore erred and should have remanded the matter to the Session. No separate merits relief beyond that remand directive appears.

2002-14.summary: A ruling elder convicted by his Session of fifth-, sixth-, and ninth-commandment violations challenged the conviction because the prosecution presented no live witness and relied on his own letters. The SJC denied the appeal and upheld Presbytery's affirmance, holding that the documents, Lachman's acknowledgments of writing them, and defense witnesses supplied sufficient proof; the Session also followed Matthew 18 with patience. A concurrence urged change-of-venue procedures for small-Session bias cases, but noted Lachman never requested a reference or challenged the court before trial.

2002-15.title: Walter Bjorck v. Northern New England Presbytery
2002-15.summary: This sparse record disposes of TE Walter Bjorck's complaint against Northern New England Presbytery as out of order; no merits opinion or reason for that ruling is published. The same minute entry also records that a request that the SJC accept and act upon the judicial reference in Case 2002-04 was not acceded to. It therefore documents only a procedural status, not the complaint's substance or the basis for the ruling.

2003-04.title: Dr. and Mrs. Frank Chin v. Covenant Presbytery
2003-04.summary: The Chins complained to the SJC after Covenant Presbytery denied their complaint against Covenant Presbyterian Church Session's refusal to examine their young children for admission to the Lord's Supper. The SJC did not sustain the complaint. Its adopted reasoning held that BCO 57-2 leaves the time for examining young persons to the Session's prudence and imposes no mandate to examine every child put forward; if the Session decides the time has come, careful examination is required. The dissent read BCO 57-1 as requiring examination of covenant children seeking admission.

2004-02.title: Nancy J. Plowman v. Philadelphia Presbytery
2004-02.summary: A member suspended from the Lord's Table appealed after Presbytery let the Session resume her trial and failed to lift all suspensions. The SJC sustained the appeal, finding the Session's premature censure, truncated trial, and prosecutor-judge conflict manifested prejudice and made a fair trial impossible. It set aside all judgments and censures, treated the November 13, 2003 communion letter as non-censuring advice, and did not remand.

2004-03.title: Tim J. Harris v. Heritage Presbytery
2004-03.summary: A church member challenged Heritage Presbytery's ruling that the BCO neither expressly nor implicitly requires a congregation to approve changes in a pastor's call, and that it does not require the session to publicize budget details. The SJC held the BCO silent on both points: once the original call and terms are approved, later changes are budgetary and belong to the session under BCO 12-5b; publicizing the budget is prudent but not mandated. The complaint was not sustained; seven commissioners dissented, arguing congregational approval follows by good and necessary consequence.

2004-05.summary: SJC sustained TE Philip Blevins's complaint against Westminster Presbytery, holding the Blevins/Seufert complaint was timely despite the commission's February 3, 2004 untimeliness ruling. The wife's April 2003 letter was essentially a BCO 35-13 request to review new evidence, and the Session's May 2003 denial was a new complaintable decision. The SJC did not decide the wife's divorce grounds or the Session's merits; it remanded for Presbytery to rehear the Session and Warhurst complaints with the Blevins/Seufert merits considered. A concurrence added that no full new trial is required.

2004-07.summary: A presbytery annulled a session's actions after the session added to a petition-called congregational meeting a recommendation that the congregation invoke BCO 24-6 against eleven elders. The SJC sustained the session's complaint: BCO 25-2 permits a session to add agenda items, and BCO 24-6 does not require a member-initiated motion; the congregation's own 503–229 vote began the process. It reinstated the session's actions, declared remaining relief moot, and noted one recorded dissent; no dissent text appears.

2004-09.title: Scott Robar v. Central Carolina Presbytery
2004-09.summary: The SJC found RE Scott Robar's appeal from Central Carolina Presbytery judicially out of order and dismissed it because he filed his notice of appeal only with Presbytery's stated clerk, not also with the General Assembly's stated clerk as BCO 42-4 requires. No merits review of his conviction occurred. Four commissioners dissented, arguing that the presbytery clerk's admittedly incorrect advice, Robar's reliance, and Presbytery's request to treat the appeal as timely should excuse the filing defect under the Plowman precedent and equity or estoppel principles.

2005-06.summary: The Standing Judicial Commission, as recorded in the 34th Assembly, found RE Hugo Andrino's complaint against Southern Florida Presbytery out of order. The supplied record includes no separate merits opinion, no adopted reason, and no relief; it does not identify the challenged presbytery action or classify the out-of-order ruling.

2006-07.title: Michael Chastain v. Heritage Presbytery
2006-07.summary: Chastain appealed Heritage Presbytery’s 2006 excommunication and deposition. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order because Chastain had renounced PCA jurisdiction on May 8, 2006. Consequently, Presbytery’s later proceedings were moot and SJC 2005-1 remained in effect. The SJC did not reach the merits. A concurrence questioned the discipline process after renunciation; a dissent argued the majority lacked constitutional authority to recognize unilateral withdrawal and thereby undercut discipline.

2007-03.summary: The 36th Assembly (2008), on the SJC docket, recorded the complaint of Greg Segallis et al. against Central Florida Presbytery as out of order (36-31, p. 75). No separate merits opinion or reason for the out-of-order disposition appears in the supplied record; the stub supports only that disposition.

2007-11.summary: After Korean Eastern Presbytery tried, convicted, deposed, and excommunicated TE Eliot Lee, the SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the disposition and excommunication. The decisive reason was procedural: the record did not show timely service of the indictment/citations or the required 14-day trial notice, violating BCO 32-3, 32-7, and 32-10. Under BCO 42-9, the SJC rendered the decision it thought should have been made, finding no strong presumption of guilt under BCO 31-2 justified formal process; it added pastoral counsel, expressly not censure.

2008-06.summary: The SJC found RE H. Lance Acree's complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery out of order. The stub records no issue, merits opinion, reasoning, or relief, and groups 2008-06 with three other 2008 cases found out of order. The complaint therefore ended without a merits determination.

2008-14.summary: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

2009-07.summary: The SJC denied James Urish and others' complaint against Rocky Mountain Presbytery for sustaining Dan Breed's ordination exam. Breed had said women could teach Scripture to mixed adults in settings like Sunday school under session oversight, but not preach, hold elder office, or teach outside session authority. Because the Westminster Standards and BCO did not expressly resolve that view, the SJC found no clear error under BCO 39 and affirmed Presbytery's denial. A concurrence criticized Breed's exegesis of 1 Tim. 2:12 but stressed the SJC was not endorsing it.

2009-14.summary: The Ellisville PC Session’s complaint against Grace Presbytery was withdrawn, and the 38th Assembly recorded that disposition (38-31, p. 129). The stub publishes no merits opinion and states no reason for the withdrawal; the case therefore supplies no ruling on the complaint’s underlying dispute.

2009-22.summary: The SJC denied a censured husband's complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery's approval of a judicial commission report, which had upheld his session's refusal to receive his charges against his wife after she filed for civil divorce. Applying BCO 39-3.2–3.3, the SJC deferred to the lower courts' factual and discretionary findings absent clear error. It found no clear procedural error, upheld the conclusion that the wife did not sin by seeking civil protection, and invoked BCO 31-8's caution about accusations from one under censure.

2009-23.summary: Illiana Presbytery appointed a commission with broad power 'to deal with matters' at Center Grove Presbyterian Church after a pastor requested inquiry into alleged evils. The SJC sustained the complaint but held the error harmless: the broad charge could take original jurisdiction from the session contrary to BCO 11-3 & 4 and 33-1, while a limited investigative committee under BCO 13-9(f) and 31-2 would have been proper. Because the commission never exercised that power and the session endorsed its findings, no remedy, including invalidation of the adopted report, was ordered.

2009-27.summary: A complaint against Platte Valley Presbytery was ruled administratively out of order by the Standing Judicial Commission at the 38th Assembly (2010), 38-31, p. 129. The published record is only a stub: it gives no merits opinion, no allegations, and no rationale for the administrative ruling, and it states no further proceedings.

2009-29.summary: McNeil v. Chesapeake, Case 2009-29, appears in the 38th General Assembly (2010) record as one of several 2009-2010 cases found administratively out of order; no separate SJC merits opinion was published. The available stub supplies no issue description, procedural-vehicle statement, or reasons for the administrative disposition, so it supports only a status synopsis, not the underlying dispute or ruling rationale.

2009-32.summary: Russell Warren’s complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery was found administratively out of order by the Standing Judicial Commission at the 38th Assembly. The supplied source gives no merits opinion, no issue-level ruling, and no adopted reason for the administrative disposition; it leaves the underlying complaint and any relief unaddressed.

2010-01.summary: Michael McNeil’s complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery was dismissed without a merits ruling after McNeil failed to appear at the SJC hearing. The panel called his name outside the hearing room and the Stated Clerk’s office; he was absent and had filed no brief. The notice had warned under BCO 42-11 that an appellant’s failure to appear would be treated as abandonment. The SJC declared the case abandoned and dismissed it. This illustrates dismissal for nonappearance, not adjudication of the underlying complaint.

2010-03.summary: An appellant under suspension from the sacraments challenged the presbytery's judicial commission process and censure. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order—not decided on the merits—because he had not submitted to a regular trial, as BCO 42-2 requires. Treated as a complaint, it was also out of order: it had not first been presented to the presbytery, and the 30-day period had expired. The SJC further barred complaints about later court actions while he remained under censure, except as to the highest censure. The censure stood.

2010-04.summary: A complaint challenged Siouxlands Presbytery's investigation of allegations that TE Joshua Moon held heterodox Federal Vision views and its finding of no strong presumption of guilt. The SJC held that Presbytery had investigated diligently under BCO 31-2 and, deferring under BCO 39-3 to its credibility judgment, found no clear error. It declined to decide whether the overture should have been treated as charges because that issue was not raised below, while leaving future charges possible. A concurrence favored charges; the dissent would have found error and remanded.

2010-07.summary: Mr. Sang Chui Choi and others brought a case against Korean Central Presbytery. The Standing Judicial Commission, in the 39th General Assembly (2011), found 2010-07 administratively out of order, listing it among seven cases (2009-29, 2009-30, 2009-31, 2010-06, 2010-07, 2010-17, 2010-25) disposed of on that ground. No separate merits opinion was published, and the adopted record gives no reason for the ruling or any underlying facts.

2010-24.summary: A complaint challenging Northwest Georgia Presbytery’s denial of Laura Wood’s complaint against a session was declared judicially out of order and dismissed because Presbytery later rescinded the challenged action; the SJC said the defects could not be cured and no grounds remained. It reached no merits. The dissent argued rescission did not automatically defeat a complaint and that her complaint also alleged Presbytery’s failure to act.

2011-01.summary: A complaint challenged the nonacceptance of charges filed with Korean Central Presbytery. The record was unclear whether Presbytery or only its clerk had refused them, and did not show that Presbytery had denied a complaint concerning that refusal. The SJC therefore held the complaint administratively out of order as premature under BCO 43-2, without reaching the merits.

2011-02.summary: The SJC denied a minister's complaint challenging Presbytery's out-of-order dismissal of his request for a BCO 31-2 investigation of another minister. Although the SJC agreed Presbytery wrongly said it had already decided all issues—the earlier complaint (SJC 2010-28) was distinct—it upheld the refusal to investigate. The accused minister had delivered an authorized committee report as chairman; absent evidence he exceeded that authorization, his statements were the committee's, not personal, and BCO 31-2 did not require investigation.

2011-05.summary: The SJC held Young Bae Kim's complaint against Korean Capital Presbytery administratively out of order because it was not filed with the Stated Clerk within 30 days after the presbytery's October 4, 2010 meeting, as BCO 43 requires. The adopted ruling reached no merits. The roll call adopted 18 concurring, 1 disqualified, and 5 absent; the disqualified commissioner could not certify that he had read the necessary record portions.

2011-06.summary: Elders complained that Missouri Presbytery erred in its BCO 31-2 investigation by finding insufficient evidence to raise a strong presumption of guilt that TE Jeffrey Meyers held Federal Vision views contrary to the Westminster Standards. The SJC answered yes: MOP erred under BCO 34-5, and the ordinary remedy was compliance with BCO 31-2. But because MOP had already tried Meyers on April 13–14, 2012, the SJC held further action moot, ordering no additional relief. Adopted by the SJC as a whole, with one dissent.

2011-10.summary: The SJC held Frank Testa's complaint against South Florida Presbytery administratively out of order because the presbytery had not yet acted on the underlying matter, so no merits decision was reached. The case thus turns on prematurity rather than the complaint's substance; the sparse record does not describe the underlying dispute. The adopted vote was 19 concurring, 1 not qualified, and 4 absent. RE Donohoe was not qualified because he could not certify that he had read the necessary portions of the Record (OMSJC 2.3.b).

2011-13.summary: An individual appealed directly to the SJC, alleging her church effectively excommunicated her without process, failed the Matthew 18 process, and spiritually abused her by social isolation. The SJC dismissed as premature, without reaching the merits, because there was no record of a judicial decision by the church or of an appeal to Evangel Presbytery, the next higher court; it stated she could proceed only by providing such evidence. The severity of excommunication did not excuse that prerequisite. The SJC asked Presbytery to obtain the session's written response to her letter.

2011-14.summary: Philadelphia Presbytery declared Reese and Bech's complaint out of order because some supporting reasons and requested amends allegedly violated the BCO. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding Presbytery misapplied Robert's Rules: objectionable parts do not justify rejecting an entire complaint, and a court need not adopt requested amends. It also said pertinent questions about whether a call is for the good of the Church may be asked, but agreed the amends—including removing TE Hsu—were inappropriate and could not rescind his installation.

2011-19.summary: Mr. Frank Testa's case against Southern Florida Presbytery was found administratively out of order by the 40th General Assembly, a procedural disposition rather than a merits ruling. No separate merits opinion was published, and the source does not identify the challenged action, grounds, or rationale. It lists 2011-19 among cases found administratively out of order, while another case was found judicially out of order.

2012-01.summary: The SJC dismissed a complaint against James River Presbytery without reaching the merits, holding it judicially out of order because the action complained against was not in the Record of the Case (BCO 43-1; OMSJC 10.6). The adopted ruling gives no further rationale and carried 13 concurring, 5 dissenting, 1 abstaining, 1 disqualified, and 4 absent. A dissent argued the record did contain an adjudicable Session action and that the cited OMSJC provision did not list the ground used; a separate written objection challenged a panel member's participation.

2012-04.summary: The SJC held TE Dwight Dunn's complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1 and directed Presbytery to remedy the deficiencies by its next Stated Meeting before further action under OMSJC 9.2. The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

2012-05.summary: The SJC denied RE Gerald Hedman's complaint against Pacific Northwest Presbytery, which had adopted five not-guilty judgments on charges that TE Peter Leithart's baptism, covenant, imputation, justification, and union-with-Christ views contradicted the Westminster Standards. Bound to the record and clear-error review, the SJC found no procedural violation and insufficient evidence that Presbytery clearly erred. It left the verdicts undisturbed, declined to endorse Leithart's views generally, and urged continued clarification of his non-standard terminology. A separate dissent would have found error and ordered a new trial or reference.

2012-06.summary: The SJC held Complaint 2012-06 administratively out of order because it was not filed within thirty days (BCO 43-2; OMSJC 18.10.b) and because the complainant, a Deacon who was not a commissioner to Presbytery at the time of the challenged action, lacked standing (BCO 43-1). No merits review appears; the adopted vote was 18 concurring, 2 not qualified, and 4 absent.

2012-09.summary: The SJC held TE M. Jay Bennett’s complaint against Missouri Presbytery administratively out of order for lack of standing. Bennett was a PCA member when he complained to Presbytery on April 16, 2012, but was received by the OPC on April 28, 2012; when he filed with the SJC on August 16, 2012, he was no longer a PCA member. The SJC reached no merits issue. The vote was 15 concurring, 2 dissenting, 1 disqualified, 1 not qualified, 1 recused, and 4 absent; no dissent rationale is stated.

2012-10.summary: The 40th General Assembly cited Korean Capital Presbytery for failing to respond to substantive exceptions in its October 6, 2008 minutes. The SJC noted that the Presbytery had submitted responses approved by the Presbytery under BCO 10-4 and found those responses acceptable. The record does not state a dismissal, acquittal, or other formal merits disposition; the matter is an administrative BCO 40-5 citation resolved by acceptance of the Presbytery's responses.

2013-01.summary: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

2013-02.summary: The 42nd General Assembly (2014) found Case 2013-02, a complaint by RE Warren Jackson against Northwest Georgia Presbytery, Administratively Out of Order. No merits opinion was published, and the surviving record gives no facts, grounds, adopted reasoning, or relief. The same disposition was entered in companion Case 2013-05, while Case 2013-09 was withdrawn as prematurely filed.

2013-07.summary: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

2013-09.summary: The 42nd Assembly (2014) disposed of Mr. G. Rick Marshall's appeal against Pacific Presbytery by withdrawal. No separate merits opinion was published, so the source does not disclose the challenged conduct, adopted reasoning, or relief beyond the withdrawal.

2013-10.summary: A presbytery deposed a minister for violating his seventh vow by pursuing an unbiblical divorce after he filed a civil petition. The SJC sustained the appeal in part: the presbytery clearly erred in finding sin in the filing, because the record did not conclusively show intent to divorce rather than protect his children, and the wife's counter-filing undermined the failure-to-withdraw inference. The SJC rejected prejudice, irregularity, and venue claims, voided the trial judgment, and noted that his expired prior suspension left him a presbytery member without call. Divorce precedents are fact-specific.

2013-12.summary: G. Rick Marshall appealed Pacific Presbytery, which failed to transmit a material part of the Record of the Case, causing irremediable injury. The SJC did not reach the merits; it suspended the lower judgment indefinitely, dismissed the appeal under BCO 42-7, rebuked Pacific Presbytery, and urged greater care in preserving, transcribing, and transmitting testimony. Dismissal therefore did not leave the challenged judgment enforceable. A separate concurrence suggested recording testimony or hiring a court reporter and questioned imprudent prosecutions.

2014-01.summary: Two ministers complained that Ohio Valley Presbytery erred by judging TE Charles Hickey's difference with Larger Catechism 177—over restricting the Lord's Supper to those able to examine themselves—as more than semantic but neither hostile to the system nor vital to religion. The SJC neither sustained nor denied the complaint. Because the Record did not sufficiently address Hickey's particular expression and rationale, the Commission remanded to Presbytery for further hearing and a fuller record. It reserved the merits, including whether this formulation of paedocommunion is allowable.

2015-01.summary: The SJC held that a ruling elder’s complaint was administratively out of order and could not be put in order because the original complaint was filed 78 days after the challenged Session action—18 days beyond BCO 43-2’s 60-day window. A second complaint was merely an extension of the untimely first. Even though Session and Presbytery recognized the untimeliness but addressed it anyway, the SJC voided all lower-court actions on the complaints. A cited 2001 case was similar.

2015-02.summary: An unsigned complaint challenging a January 21 presbytery action was sent to the PCA Clerk by someone without standing. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1.a and dismissed it: the minister with standing failed to notify the Clerk within BCO 43-3’s 30-day window, and his later e-mail was not an unqualified ratification. Because the complaint could not be put in order, the SJC reached no merits. The decision illustrates strict filing and ratification requirements.

2015-03.summary: In Complaint 2015-03, Steve Flesher and Randy Weekly challenged Metro Atlanta Presbytery, but the SJC did not reach the merits. Because the issues raised had already been adjudicated in Appeal 2015-08, the SJC declared Complaint 2015-03 moot and approved that disposition. The short decision thus records a mootness ruling based on prior appellate adjudication; the underlying presbytery action and the Appeal 2015-08 decision are not described in the supplied text.

2015-07.summary: The SJC dismissed John B. Thompson's complaint against South Florida Presbytery as administratively out of order and prematurely filed. Because BCO 43-2 did not require the presbytery to consider the complaint until its next stated meeting, and that meeting had not yet occurred, the SJC held the case could not be put in order under the BCO or OMSJC. The unanimous officers' recommendation also called Thompson's BCO 40-5 application premature. No merits were reached.

2015-08.summary: TE John Hardie appealed his Metro Atlanta Presbytery conviction on three charges of breaking ordination vows and indefinite suspension, alleging seventeen procedural and evidentiary errors. Applying BCO 39-2/3 clear-error deference, the SJC denied every specification and upheld the judgment and censure. It found no clear error in the BCO 31-2 investigation, indictment/prosecutor process, commission membership, evidence rulings, scheduling, alleged prejudice, or censure. It assessed transcription costs equally while encouraging MAP to absorb them, and cautioned that an absent commissioner's vote might support a future challenge.

2015-09.summary: A claimant sought BCO 40-5 review of Presbytery’s handling of his earlier judicial case, alleging grossly unconstitutional proceedings and delinquency in failing to investigate his 2012 deposition. The SJC found the application administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order because BCO 40-3 excludes judicial-case proceedings from review and control when notice of appeal or complaint has been given, and he had withdrawn his 2012 complaint acknowledging it could not be resubmitted. It dismissed under OMSJC 9.2(d). The concurrence added that BCO 40 cannot refile a withdrawn complaint or reverse a censure.

2015-12.summary: After Metro Atlanta Presbytery dissolved Grace North Atlanta, a complaint challenging that action was declared administratively out of order for lacking a signature. Wills then complained to the SJC. The SJC held the SJC complaint was not properly before it and was administratively out of order: under BCO 43-2, a complaint must first go to the court whose act is challenged, and Presbytery had not yet addressed that ruling. Wills could file with Presbytery within 30 days. No merits ruling on the dissolution.

2015-13.summary: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

2016-02.summary: The SJC found TE Arnold Robertstad's complaint against North Texas Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order under BCO 43-3. Robertstad initially filed by e-mail—not an allowed filing—and his hard-copy filing arrived after the thirty-day deadline. The SJC reasoned that BCO 42-4/43-3 notification language concerns a lower court notifying parties, not party e-filing, and OMSJC 18.10.b bars e-mail filing. The merits were not reached; a concurrence urged later clarification by amendment, and no further proceedings are indicated.

2016-07.summary: Avery and Lewelling complained that Nashville Presbytery wrongly denied their complaint against Shepherding Committee actions: initiating an investigation of TE Jim Bachmann and forwarding the report to the Committee on Judicial Business. The SJC dismissed. The November 10, 2015 challenge was untimely under BCO 43-2's 60-day filing rule; the February 9, 2016 challenge was not a proper complaint because it targeted committee activities, not a court's act or decision. All specifications were judicially out of order and could not be put in order.

2016-08.summary: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

2016-12.summary: Complainants sought review of Nashville Presbytery's August 9, 2016 actions but filed directly with the SJC instead of first with Presbytery. The SJC held the complaint judicially out of order and unable to be put in order: the initial filing was not a complaint against an act or decision (BCO 43-1) but suggested charges or an investigation request (BCO 31-2); BCO 43-2 required prior filing with Presbytery, and the sixty-day period had run. The complaint was dismissed without a merits ruling.

2016-15.summary: TE James Bachmann appealed Nashville Presbytery's decision to replace his judicial commission's recommended admonition with indefinite suspension. The SJC sustained the appeal: Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by dividing the verdict and amending the censure, which it had to approve or disapprove as a whole without debate. Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. The SJC rendered the commission's judgment and admonition as its own decision, remanded to Presbytery, and restored Bachmann to good standing, subject to possible pastoral oversight items 2–4.

2016-16.summary: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

2016-17.summary: Did Heritage Presbytery err by cautioning a session and requesting that it postpone a candidate's election or ordination while a complaint about his qualifications was pending? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. The motion was advice, not an act for or requirement imposed on the session; the session could disregard it, and BCO 43-2 does not bar presbyters from discussing matters related to a complaint not yet before them. The SJC left undecided whether such discussions would disqualify presbyters, since the Ullrey complaint never reached presbytery.

2017-01.summary: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

2017-02.summary: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Heritage Presbytery’s November 12, 2016 action charging a teaching elder with violating ordination vows 6 and 7 and appointing a prosecutor to investigate and, if necessary, indict. The complaint alleged the investigating committee lacked authority for judicial process, no written report existed, and the procedure and wording violated BCO 31-2. The Commission held a committee recommendation is not judicial action, no special instruction was required, the BCO 31-2 steps were followed, and the wording did not violate the accused’s rights.

2017-08.title: BCO 40-5 Report of RE John B. Thompson
2017-08.summary: The SJC ruled out of order a BCO 40-5 report submitted by RE John B. Thompson, disposing of it without a separate merits opinion. The available record states no reason for the ruling and identifies no relief or further proceeding; it establishes only the out-of-order disposition, not the underlying dispute or any governing principle.

2018-04.summary: A complaint sought a congregational meeting to vote on leaving the PCA after the temporary session denied the request in November 2017. The SJC dismissed the complaint as moot and not judicially in order. Both parties agreed at the panel hearing that the presbytery had voted in October 2018 to dismiss the congregation pending consent under BCO 13-9(f), and consent was given at a December 2018 called meeting. No merits ruling was made. Three commissioners dissented; one was disqualified.

2018-05.summary: The SJC held that TE David McKay's complaint against Central Indiana Presbytery was administratively out of order. The decisive defect was procedural: the e-mail transmitted to the lower court clerk did not satisfy BCO 43-3 because the complainant's correspondence was insufficient to constitute proper notice. The SJC therefore reached no merits issue. All 24 participating commissioners concurred, with no dissent. The ruling enforces BCO 43-3's notice requirement before a complaint can proceed.

2018-06.summary: The SJC held that Jared Edwards's complaint against North Texas Presbytery was administratively out of order and could not be put in order, because the case had never been filed with the presbytery or adjudicated below (BCO 42-4 & 43-2). No merits were reached. The ruling drew 23 concurrences and no dissent; TE Fowler was disqualified as a member of the presbytery party (OMSJC 2.10(d)(3)(iii)). The decision illustrates the SJC's threshold filing requirement: a complaint that bypassed the lower court cannot proceed.

2019-02.summary: The SJC sustained a complaint against Philadelphia Presbytery for failing to judge and record TE Larry Smith’s stated difference over the continuation of prophecy and tongues beyond the apostolic era. The record showed Presbytery approved Smith’s transfer exam and defeated a motion to find his view out of accord, but it did not categorize that view in Smith’s own words. The SJC remanded for a written statement and Presbytery’s categorical judgment, without undoing Smith’s transfer or deciding whether his view was erroneous.

2019-07.summary: At issue was whether North Texas Presbytery wrongly denied a complaint challenging Fort Worth Presbyterian Church’s “Special Case Felons” integration policy as contrary to Scripture. The SJC denied the complaint, holding that the complainant did not show the Session violated Scripture or the Constitution and that BCO 39-3.3 required deference absent clear error, leaving the lower-court actions in effect. The decision, adopted 20-1, expressly did not endorse the Respondents’ Preliminary Principles arguments; a concurrence disclaimed approval of the policy, and one member dissented.

2019-09.summary: On complaint by RE William F. Mueller, the SJC reviewed whether the Redlands Community Church Session erred on January 14, 2019 by allegedly reaffirming its practice of fencing the Lord's Table contrary to BCO 58-4. The SJC denied the complaint: the only relevant motion failed for lack of a second, so the Session took no action and did not reaffirm anything. It noted the case could have been ruled out of order earlier and that Mueller could pursue relief under BCO 40-5; a concurrence stressed BCO 58-4 remains binding and criticized Presbytery's handling.

2019-14.summary: The SJC found the complaint administratively out of order and dismissed it. The complainants had not documented that they first presented the complaint to Korean Southwest Orange County Presbytery under BCO 43-2, and the SJC held that the Presbytery—not the SJC—was the proper court for the charges and specifications in the March 2, 2020 letter. The dismissal was recorded 19-0-0; no merits were reached.

2020-08.summary: The SJC sustained the complaint of TEs Gendall, Hightower, and Lien against Pacific Presbytery's handling of a BCO 38-1 confession by TE Rankin Wilbourne. Presbytery had denied the complaint. The SJC held that reading a prejudicial six-page judicial-commission report before the agreed statement of facts violated BCO 38-1 and tainted the censure. It answered the 2020-08 complaint by reference to its decision in Case 2020-07, which annulled Wilbourne's deposition and recommended treating his 17-month suspension as sufficient definite suspension.

2020-10.summary: A complaint was filed with the SJC before Savannah River Presbytery completed its hearing on it. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order as prematurely filed and did not reach the merits. It reset the complainant's time to elevate the complaint so that timing begins on the later of notification of the SJC action or Presbytery's ruling. The SJC adopted the decision by roll call.

2020-13.summary: The SJC dismissed Peter Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery as administratively out of order because he lacked standing to complain of the Presbytery's action. Benyola was neither a teaching elder member of that Presbytery nor a ruling elder commissioner representing a member church at the September 18, 2020 meeting when the Presbytery considered and denied the complaint. Citing prior SJC standing decisions, the Commission held the defect could not be cured and dismissed unanimously, 22-0-0, without reaching the merits.

2021-01.summary: The SJC held that Stuart Michelson's complaint against Northwest Georgia Presbytery was administratively out of order because he filed it with the SJC before Presbytery had completed its hearing on the complaint. The SJC did not reach the merits. It reset Michelson's time to elevate the complaint to run from the later of notification of the SJC's action or Presbytery's ruling on the complaint. Approved 22-0-0.

2021-05.summary: The SJC held an October 2021 complaint against Southwest Florida Presbytery administratively out of order because the complainants had affiliated with another branch of the visible church on February 9, 2020, ending PCA jurisdiction over them under BCO 38-3. They therefore lacked standing. The ruling reached no merits and supplies no description of the underlying presbytery action; the vote was 22-0-0, with Lucas and White absent.

2021-12.summary: The Michelsons’ complaint challenged a congregational meeting’s procedure for electing three assistant pastors as associate pastors—allegedly without a pulpit committee, ballots, counted abstentions, or protection for a substantial minority. The SJC dismissed it as not judicially in order: BCO 43-1 requires complaint against an act or decision of a court, but the complaint attacked congregational actions, while the Session’s only act was calling the meeting and was not objected to. The SJC noted other possible redress; the dissent found the Session’s call and recommendation justiciable.

2022-01.summary: The SJC dismissed Eric Eagle and others' complaint against Savannah River Presbytery as administratively out of order and untimely under BCO 43-3. The complaint was first filed prematurely in December 2020; after the SJC reset the filing clock to the later of its October 21, 2021 action or Presbytery's October 20, 2020 ruling, it was filed more than 30 days later. The merits were not reached. An attached SJC response to CCB separately defended its record-reopening in Case 2020-12 and asked CCB to deny an exception request as untimely, waived, and procedural.

2022-03.summary: Philadelphia Presbytery declared that TE Larry Smith's views on continuing prophecy and tongues were not out of accord or hostile to the system of doctrine. Klett et al. complained. The SJC sustained the complaint: Smith's written views affirmed continuing non-general revelation and treated prophecy and tongues as public-worship elements, contrary to WCF 1 and 21, so Presbytery erred under BCO 21-4.f. The SJC annulled Presbytery's May 15, 2021 action. No further action was possible because Smith and his congregation had left the PCA; the matter was concluded, with precedent limited to the written views reviewed.

2022-04.summary: The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.

2022-07.summary: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

2022-08.summary: The SJC held that RE David Snoke's complaint against Pittsburgh Presbytery's January 29, 2022 action was administratively out of order and could not be put in order because Snoke, not a commissioner from his church to that meeting, lacked standing to complain. Although Presbytery later voted 20-16-3 to find the complaint in order, the SJC said it should have been ruled out of order. The SJC did not reach the merits. Its vote was 20-1, with three absent.

2022-09.summary: The SJC declared Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order, because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The decision was adopted 23-0 on a roll call, one absent, on the officers' recommendation. The record does not identify the underlying presbytery action or reach the complaint's merits, so the case's value is its threshold standing ruling, not any complaint determination.

2022-13.summary: Wade Miller challenged his Session’s May 19, 2021 letter standing by its decision to permit a non-church yoga class to meet on church property. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order: that letter triggered BCO 43-1’s 60-day deadline, but Miller filed with the Session on November 20, 2021, and no new Session action occurred within the preceding 60 days. Citing a one-day-late precedent, the SJC reached no merits.

2022-15.summary: A complaint against South Florida Presbytery was held administratively out of order because its sole complainant died on November 15, 2022, and no other person joined the original complaint. The SJC adopted that disposition by a 23–0 roll-call vote. The sparse record states no underlying complaint issue, merits analysis, or further proceedings; the ruling turns on the absence of a surviving or joined complainant.

2022-16.summary: The SJC declined to reach a complaint arising from judicial process against three ruling elders (not the complainants), because the Session dismissed all charges and ended that process on July 23, 2022, and the elders resigned and their calls were dissolved. The SJC found the complaint out of order and moot, with no merits ruling, and approved the decision 23-0. The case illustrates that termination of the underlying judicial process and voluntary resignations can moot a complaint about that process.

2022-23.summary: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

2023-01.summary: Kristin Hann's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery was dismissed because the SJC held she lacked standing: she was not subject to Pee Dee Presbytery's jurisdiction, so the complaint was judicially out of order and could not be put in order. The SJC made no merits ruling and stated that the ruling did not stay Presbytery's continuing investigation or review of resulting actions. The adopted ruling was approved 17-2; Maynard and Sartorius dissented without stated reasons, four were absent, and Ross recused.

2023-02.summary: The SJC dismissed Mrs. Kappie Reynolds's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery as judicially out of order. The complaint challenged a Session's reception of and action on a confession at a meeting more than six months before filing, far outside BCO 43-2's sixty-day period; the SJC held the untimeliness was not demonstrated curable. The ruling expressly reserved whether Reynolds could proceed as an injured party under BCO 31-5 and whether the Session had jurisdiction over claims outside the received confession.

2023-05.summary: Former church employee Emily Hyland complained to the SJC after Chicago Metro Presbytery ruled her BCO 43 complaint out of order because, as a local-church member, she was not subject to Presbytery's jurisdiction. The SJC was equally divided 12–12–0 on the proposed panel decision, so CMP's ruling stands. That proposed decision would have answered that CMP did not err: Hyland lacked standing to file a BCO 43-1 complaint with Presbytery. No amendments were made. An evenly divided SJC thus leaves the lower ruling in place without a majority rationale.
